blocks.text: First, the Chapter on the Account of His Conduct
1. Opening the occasion and preaching the Dharma

inline.s: At that time the Master arrived at Baolin. The Prefect Wei of Shaozhou and his officials entered the mountains to ask the Master to come forth, and at the lecture hall of the Great Brahma temple in the city he opened the occasion and preached the Dharma for the assembly. When the Master had ascended the seat, over thirty officials with the Prefect, over thirty Confucian scholars, and over a thousand monks, nuns and lay followers made obeisance together, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma.
The Master said to the assembly: Good friends! The self-nature of bodhi is originally pure. Only use this mind, and directly realize Buddhahood.

blocks.text: 2. Seeking the Dharma at East Mountain

inline.s: Good friends! Listen to the account of how Huineng won the Dharma. Huineng's father, by origin of Fanyang, had been demoted and banished to Lingnan, becoming a commoner of Xinzhou. In this unfortunate body of mine the father died early, leaving my old mother widowed and alone; we moved to Nanhai and in hardship and poverty I sold firewood at the market.

At that time a certain guest bought firewood and had me deliver it to his lodging. The guest took it in, and Huineng, having received the money, went out again and saw a guest reciting a sutra. As soon as Huineng heard the words of the sutra, his mind at once awakened.
(The Caoxi original text: seeing a guest reciting the sutra, as soon as Huineng heard the words of the sutra - "should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere" - his mind at once awakened.)

He then asked the guest, "What sutra are you reciting?" The guest said, "The Diamond Sutra." He asked again, "From where do you come, and how do you have this sutra?" The guest said, "I come from East Meditation Temple in Huangmei county, Qizhou. In that temple the Fifth Patriarch, the Great Master Ren, presides and transforms, with more than a thousand disciples. I went there, paid my respects, and heard and received this sutra. The Master always urges monks and layfolk: only hold to the Diamond Sutra, and you will see your own nature and directly realize Buddhahood."

Huineng, hearing this, felt a relation from former lives; a guest then gave him ten taels of silver, to provide clothing and food for his old mother, and told him to go at once to Huangmei to pay respects to the Fifth Patriarch. Having settled his mother, Huineng took his leave. In a little over thirty days he reached Huangmei and paid respects to the Fifth Patriarch.

The Patriarch asked, "From what place have you come, and what do you seek?" Huineng replied, "Your disciple is a commoner of Xinzhou in Lingnan; I have come from afar to pay respects to the Master, seeking only to become a Buddha, seeking nothing else." The Patriarch said, "You are from Lingnan and a man of the wilds — how could you become a Buddha?" Huineng said, "Though people have south and north, the Buddha-nature originally has no south or north. The body of a man of the wilds differs from the Master's, but what difference is there in the Buddha-nature?" The Fifth Patriarch wished to speak further with him, but seeing the crowd all about, he told him to go work with the assembly.

Huineng said, "Huineng ventures to say to the Master: the wisdom of your disciple's own mind constantly arises and never leaves the self-nature — this is the field of blessing. I would ask what work the Master would teach me to do." The Patriarch said, "This man of the wilds has great keenness of root-nature. Say no more; go to the threshing room." Huineng withdrew to the back court, where a lay attendant set him to splitting firewood and treading the pestle, and over eight months passed.

One day the Patriarch suddenly saw Huineng and said, "I have been thinking your view might be of use, but I feared evil men might harm you, so I did not speak with you; do you know this?" Huineng said, "Your disciple also knows the Master's intention, and dared not approach the hall, so that no one would notice."

One day the Patriarch called all his disciples together and said, "I say to you: for worldly people the matter of birth and death is great. You spend all day seeking only the field of blessing, and do not seek to escape the bitter sea of birth and death. If the self-nature is deluded, how can a blessing save you? Go, each of you, look into your own wisdom and take the prajna nature of your own fundamental mind; each of you make a verse and bring it to show me. If you awaken to the great meaning, I will give you the robe and the Dharma and make you the Sixth Patriarch. Go quickly, and do not delay! Deliberation is of no use; for a man who sees his nature, it must be seen at the very word. One who is thus — even wielding a blade on the battlefield — would see it too."

When the assembly received this command, they withdrew and said to one another, "We all need not clear the mind and deliberately compose a verse to present to the Master; of what benefit would it be? The senior seat Shenxiu is now our instructor and teacher, so it must be he who attains it. If the rest of us recklessly make verse, we will but waste our mental effort." Hearing these words, they all abandoned the idea, saying, "Henceforth we will rely on Master Xiu; why bother to compose verses?"

Shenxiu reflected: "The reason the others do not present verses is that I am their instructor and teacher; I must compose a verse and present it to the Master. If I do not present it, how can the Master know how deep or shallow the understanding in my mind is? If I present a verse seeking the Dharma, that is good; but if I seek the patriarch's seat, that is evil — and would that not be an ordinary mind stealing the sage's place? Yet if I do not present a verse, in the end I can never attain the Dharma. It is hard! It is hard!"

Before the Fifth Patriarch's hall there was a corridor of three rooms, and it was proposed to ask the salaried artist Lu Zhen to paint the transformation-scenes of the Lankavatara Sutra and the lineage pictures of the Five Patriarchs, to be handed down and revered. When Shenxiu had completed his verse, he tried several times to present it; but as he reached the hall his mind wavered, sweat ran over his whole body, and he could not present it. Over four days, thirteen times he failed to present it. Shenxiu then thought, "Better to write it on the corridor wall and let the Master see it; if he happens to say it is good, I will come forth and bow, saying it is I who made it. If he says it is not fit for use, then I have vainly spent years in the mountains, receiving people's obeisance — what Way could I then still cultivate?"
That night at the third watch, without letting anyone know, he took up a lamp himself and wrote his verse on the wall of the south corridor, showing what his mind had seen. The verse said:
The body is the bodhi tree, the mind is a bright mirror stand;
Ever diligently wipe it clean, and let no dust settle upon it.

When Shenxiu had written his verse, he returned to his room, and no one knew of it. Shenxiu reflected again: "Tomorrow, if the Fifth Patriarch sees the verse and is delighted, then I have a relation with the Dharma; if he says it is not fit, then I am deluded and my past karma is heavy, and I am not worthy of the Dharma. The sage's intent is hard to fathom!" He brooded in his room, unable to sit or sleep at ease, until the fifth watch.

blocks.text: 4. The Fifth Patriarch sees the verse

inline.s: The Patriarch already knew that Shenxiu had not entered the gate and had not seen his self-nature. At dawn he summoned the artist Lu to paint the pictures on the wall of the south corridor, and suddenly came upon the verse. He said, "The artist need not paint; we have troubled you to come from afar. The sutra says: 'All marks are false and vain.' Leave this verse here, that people may recite and hold it. Cultivating in accord with this verse, one avoids falling into evil destinies; cultivating in accord with this verse, one gains great benefit." He told the disciples, "Burn incense and pay reverence, and all recite this verse, and you will see your nature." The disciples, reciting the verse, all sighed, "Excellent!"

At the third watch the Patriarch summoned Shenxiu into the hall and asked, "Did you make this verse?" Shenxiu said, "It is indeed I who made it; I dare not vainly seek the patriarch's seat. I only hope the Master, in his compassion, will see whether your disciple has a little wisdom." The Patriarch said, "By this verse you have not yet seen the fundamental nature, having reached only the gate and not entered within. With such an understanding you can in no way attain supreme bodhi. Supreme bodhi requires that at the very word you know your own fundamental mind, and see that your fundamental nature is neither born nor destroyed; at all times, thought after thought, seeing it yourself, with all dharmas unobstructed. When the one is true, all is true; all realms are as they are, and this as-it-is mind is the real. If you see it thus, this is the self-nature of supreme bodhi. Go back and reflect for a day or two, and make another verse to bring me. If your verse enters the gate, I will give you the robe and the Dharma." Shenxiu made obeisance and went out. After several more days he could not compose a verse; his mind was wavering, his spirit uneasy, as in a dream, unhappy whether walking or sitting.

Two days later, a youth passed by the mill chanting that verse. As soon as Huineng heard it, he knew this verse had not seen the fundamental nature. Though he had not yet received instruction, he already recognized the gist. He asked the youth, "What verse is it you are reciting?" The youth said, "You man of the wilds do not know! The Master said that for worldly people the matter of birth and death is great, and wishing to transmit the robe and the Dharma, he has the disciples compose verses to show him; whoever awakens to the great meaning he will give the robe and the Dharma and make the Sixth Patriarch. The senior seat Shenxiu has written a formless verse on the wall of the south corridor, and the Master has everyone recite it. Cultivating in accord with this verse, one avoids falling into evil destinies; cultivating in accord with this verse, one gains great benefit." Huineng said, "I too wish to recite it, to form a relation for a future life, and be reborn together in the Buddha-ground. Worthy sir! I have trodden this mill for over eight months and never been to the hall; I beg you to lead me before the verse to pay reverence."

The youth led him before the verse, and he paid reverence. Huineng said, "Huineng cannot read; may the worthy sir read it for me." At that time there was a deputy of Jiangzhou, by surname Zhang and name Riyong, who read it aloud. Huineng, having heard it, said, "I too have a verse; may the deputy write it for me." The deputy said, "You can also compose a verse! That is a rare thing!" Huineng said to the deputy, "To learn supreme bodhi, one must not slight the beginning student. The lowest of the low may hold the highest of wisdom; the highest of the high may have wisdom that goes astray. To despise others is to incur immeasurable, boundless offense." The deputy said, "Only recite your verse; I will write it for you. If you attain the Dharma, be sure first to ferry me across, and forget not this word." Huineng's verse said:
Bodhi is no tree at all, the bright mirror no stand;
From the first not one thing is; where can the dust land?

When this verse had been written, the whole assembly was astonished, and they all gasped, saying to one another, "How wonderful! One must not judge a person by his appearance. How could he have been here so long, and yet be a bodhisattva of flesh and blood?" The Patriarch, seeing the crowd alarmed and startled, and fearing someone might harm him, wiped the verse off with his shoe, saying, "He too has not seen the nature." The assembly took this as so.

blocks.text: 6. Transmitting the Dharma at the third watch

inline.s: The next day the Patriarch went secretly to the mill and saw Huineng grinding rice with a stone at his waist. He said, "One who seeks the Way, for the Dharma forgetting his body — he should be thus, should he not!" He then asked, "Is the rice ready yet?" Huineng said, "The rice has long been ready! It still awaits the sifting." The Patriarch struck the mortar three times with his staff and left. Huineng at once understood the Patriarch's intent, and at the third drum entered his room. The Patriarch, covering him round with the kasaya so that no one could see, preached the Diamond Sutra for him. At the words "should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere," Huineng was greatly awakened, understanding that all dharmas do not leave the self-nature. He then said to the Patriarch, "How unexpected that the self-nature is originally pure! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally neither born nor destroyed! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally complete in itself! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally unmoving! How unexpected that the self-nature gives rise to all dharmas!" The Patriarch, knowing he had awakened to his fundamental nature, said to Huineng, "Without knowing the fundamental mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit. If you know your own fundamental mind and see your own fundamental nature, you are called a great man, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha."

Receiving the Dharma at the third watch, unknown to anyone, he was then given the Sudden Teaching and the robe and bowl, with these words: "You are the Sixth Patriarch. Guard it well with mindfulness, ferry widely those who have feeling, and let it flow into the future without interruption! Hear my verse:
In the sentient the seed is sown; upon the ground the fruit is grown;
The insentient no seed shall own; where no nature is, nothing is born."

The Patriarch continued, "Long ago the Great Master Bodhidharma first came to this land, and the people did not yet believe in him, so he transmitted this robe as the token of the faith, handed down from generation to generation. As to the Dharma, it is transmitted from mind to mind, each causing one to self-awaken and self-understand. From ancient times the Buddhas have transmitted only the fundamental body, and the masters have secretly entrusted the fundamental mind. The robe is a cause of contention — with you, do not transmit it. If you transmit this robe, your life will hang by a thread. You must go quickly, lest men harm you." Huineng asked, "To where shall I go?" The Patriarch said, "When you meet Huai, stay; when you meet Hui, hide."

At the third watch Huineng received the robe and bowl, and said, "Huineng is from the south and has never known these mountain paths; how shall I get out to the mouth of the river?" The Fifth Patriarch said, "You need not grieve; I myself will see you off." The Patriarch accompanied him to the Jiujiang post station, where he had Huineng board the boat and himself took the oars and rowed. Huineng said, "Pray, Master, be seated; your disciple should row." The Patriarch said, "It is fitting that I should ferry you across." Huineng said, "When deluded, the master ferries one across; when awakened, one ferries oneself. The name is one, but the use is different. Huineng was born in a border region, and my speech is not proper, yet I have received the Dharma through the Master. Now that I am awakened, I should ferry myself across by my own nature." The Patriarch said, "So it is! So it is! From now on the Buddha-Dharma will be greatly spread by you. Three years after you go, I shall pass away. Now go well, and strive toward the south. Do not preach too soon; the Buddha-Dharma is hard to raise up."

After taking leave of the Patriarch, Huineng set off southward, and in the course of two months reached Dayu Ridge. Several hundred men came after him, wanting to seize the robe and bowl. One monk, whose family name was Chen and whose name was Huiming, had formerly been a general of the fourth rank and was of rough and coarse nature; he sought with utmost determination, and being first of the crowd, overtook Huineng.

Huineng threw the robe and bowl upon a rock and said, "This robe is a sign of faith; can it be won by force?" He hid in the thick grass. When Huiming arrived he could not lift them, so he called out, "Practitioner! Practitioner! I have come for the Dharma, not for the robe." Huineng then came out and sat upon a flat rock. Huiming made obeisance and said, "I pray the practitioner to speak the Dharma for me." Huineng said, "Since you have come for the Dharma, put aside all conditions and do not give rise to a single thought; I will speak it for you." After a long while Huineng said, "Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil — at just such a moment, what is the original face of Senior Huiming?" At that word Huiming was greatly awakened.

He asked again, "Apart from the secret words and secret meaning just now, is there yet further secret meaning?" Huineng said, "What has been spoken to you is not secret; if you turn the light back within, the secret is on your side." Huiming said, "Though Huiming was at Huangmei, he truly never knew his own face. Now that I have received this instruction, it is like a man drinking water who knows for himself whether it is cold or warm; now the practitioner is Huiming's teacher!" Huineng said, "If it is so, you and I share the same master at Huangmei; cultivate well and keep it!" Huiming asked again, "Where shall Huiming go from now on?" Huineng said, "When you meet Yuan, stay; when you meet Meng, dwell." Huiming bowed and took his leave.

Huineng later arrived at Caoxi, but was again pursued and sought by evil men. So at Sihui he took refuge in a band of hunters and hid from the trouble for fifteen years. From time to time he spoke the Dharma to the hunters as occasion allowed; the hunters would have him watch the nets, and whenever he saw a living thing he always released it. At mealtime he would cook his vegetables in the same pot as the hunters' meat, and when asked, replied, "I only eat the vegetables by the meat."

blocks.text: 9. The Way accomplished, he leaves the mountains

inline.s: One day he thought, "The time has come to spread the Dharma; I must not hide forever." He then came forth, and arrived at the Faxing temple in Guangzhou, where he met the Dharma Master Yinzong preaching the Nirvana Sutra. At that time the wind stirred a banner, and one monk said, "The wind moves," and another monk said, "The banner moves." They argued without end. Huineng came forward and said, "It is not the wind moving, it is not the banner moving — it is your minds that move, good sirs." The whole assembly was startled.

Yinzong invited him to the first seat and questioned him on the profound meaning; seeing that Huineng's words were concise and the principle right, and that he did not depend on words, Yinzong said, "The practitioner is certainly no ordinary man. I have long heard that the robe and Dharma of Huangmei have come south — could it be you, practitioner?" Huineng said, "I dare not!" Yinzong thereupon made obeisance, and asked that the transmitted robe and bowl be shown to the great assembly.

Yinzong asked again, "What was the entrustment of Huangmei, and how was it instructed?" Huineng said, "There is no instruction; it only speaks of seeing the nature, and does not speak of meditation or liberation." Yinzong said, "Why does it not speak of meditation and liberation?" Huineng said, "Because these are two dharmas and are not the Buddha-Dharma; the Buddha-Dharma is the Dharma of non-duality." Yinzong asked again, "What is this Dharma of non-duality of the Buddha-Dharma?"

Huineng said, "The Dharma Master preaches the Nirvana Sutra and makes clear that the Buddha-nature is the Dharma of non-duality of the Buddha-Dharma. For example, the Bodhisattva King of Noble Virtue said to the Buddha: When one commits the four grave offenses, does the five deadly offenses, and is an icchantika — is the root of good and the Buddha-nature cut off? The Buddha said: The root of good is twofold — the one permanent, the other impermanent. The Buddha-nature is neither permanent nor impermanent, therefore it is not cut off, and this is called non-duality. There is the good and the not-good; the Buddha-nature is neither good nor not-good, and this is called non-duality. The aggregates and the elements — the ordinary man sees them as two; the wise, understanding through and through, see that their nature is non-dual. The nature of non-duality is the Buddha-nature."

blocks.text: 11. Opening and spreading the Sudden Teaching

inline.s: On hearing this, Yinzong was delighted, put his palms together and said, "My preaching of sutras is like broken tiles and pebbles; the worthy's discussion of principle is like true gold." He then shaved the head of Huineng and wished to serve him as his teacher. Huineng thereupon, beneath the bodhi tree, opened the East Mountain gate of the Dharma.

Huineng, having attained the Dharma at East Mountain, endured every hardship, his life hanging by a thread. Today to be in this assembly with the Prefect, the officials, the monks, nuns and layfolk — is this not the relation of numberless eons, and the sowing of good roots in former lives through making offerings to all the Buddhas, that at last we can hear the cause of the above Sudden Teaching and its attainment? This teaching is handed down by the former sages, not the wisdom of Huineng himself. Let those who wish to hear the teaching of the former sages each purify the mind; and having heard, let each remove his doubts, to be no different from the sages of old.
The whole assembly, hearing the Dharma, rejoiced, made obeisance and withdrew.
The next day the Prefect Wei sought further instruction. The Master ascended the seat and said to the great assembly: Purify your minds all together, and recite Maha-Prajna-Paramita.

Again he said: Good friends! The wisdom of bodhi-prajna is originally possessed by all people, but because the mind is deluded they cannot awaken to it themselves; they must rely on a great good friend to show and guide them to see the nature. You should know that the Buddha-nature of the fool and the wise is originally undifferentiated, and only because of the difference of delusion and awakening are there the dull and the quick. Now I shall preach the Dharma of Maha-Prajna-Paramita for you, that each may attain wisdom. Listen with your whole heart; I will speak for you.

Good friends! People all day long recite prajna with their mouths, yet do not know the self-nature prajna — it is like speaking of food yet never eating. If the mouth only speaks of emptiness, in a hundred thousand eons one cannot see the nature, and in the end it is of no benefit.

Good friends! Maha-Prajna-Paramita is Sanskrit; in the speech of Tang it is great wisdom reaching the other shore. This must be practiced with the mind, not spoken with the mouth. To speak it with the mouth while not practicing it with the mind is like illusion, like transformation, like dew, like lightning; but to speak it with the mouth and practice it with the mind is for mind and mouth to be in accord. The fundamental nature is the Buddha; apart from the nature there is no other Buddha.

What is called maha? Maha is great. The capacity of the mind is vast, like empty space, with no bounds, no square or round, no great or small, no blue, yellow, red or white, no above or below, no long or short, no anger or joy, no right or wrong, no good or evil, no head or tail.
The lands of all Buddhas are alike empty space. The wondrous nature of people is fundamentally empty, and not a single dharma can be obtained. The true emptiness of the self-nature is likewise.

Good friends! Do not, on hearing me speak of emptiness, then attach to emptiness. Above all do not attach to emptiness! If one empties the mind and sits in stillness, one attaches to the emptiness of indeterminacy.

Good friends! The emptiness of the world can hold all the forms of things — the sun, moon, stars and constellations, the mountains, rivers and the great earth, springs, sources, streams and valleys, grass and trees and thickets, evil men and good men, evil dharmas and good dharmas, heavens and hells, all the great seas, all the Sumeru mountains — all are within the emptiness. The emptiness of the nature of people is likewise.

Good friends! That the self-nature can contain all dharmas is the great — all dharmas are within the nature of all people. If one sees both the evil and the good of all people, taking none up and rejecting none, and is not defiled by them, having a mind like empty space, this is called great; therefore it is called maha.

Good friends! The deluded speak with the mouth; the wise practice with the mind. There are also the deluded who empty the mind and sit in stillness, thinking of nothing at all, and call themselves great; with this kind of people one cannot speak, because of their wrong views.

Good friends! The vast capacity of the mind pervades the whole Dharma-realm. In function it is clearly distinct, and in responding it knows all things. All is one, and one is all. Going and coming freely, the mind-substance without obstruction — this is prajna.

Good friends! All prajna wisdom is born from the self-nature and does not enter from without; do not misdirect your intention. This is the self-use of the true nature, the one real being all real. The vast matter of the mind does not walk the small path. Do not all day speak of emptiness with the mouth, while within the mind you do not practice this practice — that is like a common man calling himself a king, which can never be obtained, and such a one is not my disciple.

Good friends! What is called prajna? Prajna, in the language of Tang, is wisdom. In every place and at every time, thought after thought without delusion, ever practicing wisdom — this is the practice of prajna. In a single thought of delusion prajna is cut off; in a single thought of wisdom prajna is born. Worldly people, deluded and confused, do not see prajna; they speak of prajna with the mouth, while the mind is ever deluded, and they constantly say they cultivate prajna, thought after thought speaking of emptiness, yet not knowing the true emptiness. Prajna has no form or mark; the wisdom mind itself is it. If one understands it thus, it is called prajna wisdom.

What is called paramita? This is a word of the western regions; in the speech of Tang it means reaching the other shore, understanding the meaning of leaving birth and death. When one attaches to objects, birth and death arise, as water has waves — this is called this shore; when apart from objects there is no birth and death, as water flows ever through — this is called the other shore. Hence it is named paramita.

Good friends! When the deluded recite with the mouth, at the time of recitation there is falsehood and wrongness. If thought after thought one practices it, this is called the true nature. One who awakens to this method is in the prajna Dharma; one who practices this practice is in the prajna practice. Not to practice — that is the ordinary man; in a single thought of practice, one's own body is equal to the Buddha.

Good friends! The ordinary man is the Buddha; affliction is bodhi. With a former thought deluded, one is the ordinary man; with a later thought awakened, one is a Buddha. With a former thought attached to objects, there is affliction; with a later thought apart from objects, there is bodhi.
Good friends!
Maha-prajna-paramita, most honored, highest, first;
No abiding, no going, no coming — from it the Buddhas of three times burst.

One should use great wisdom to break through the five aggregates, affliction and the dust of toil. Cultivating thus, one is certain to accomplish the Buddha-way, transforming the three poisons into precepts, concentration and wisdom.

Good friends! In this Dharma-gate of mine, from one prajna are born eighty-four thousand wisdoms. Why? Because worldly people have eighty-four thousand kinds of dust and toil. If there were no dust and toil, wisdom would ever appear and never leave the self-nature. One who awakens to this method is without thought, without recollection, without attachment. Not giving rise to falsehood and deceit, and using one's own true-tathata nature, with wisdom contemplating and illuminating, taking nothing up and rejecting nothing among all dharmas — this is seeing the nature and accomplishing the Buddha-way.

Good friends! If you wish to enter the profound Dharma-realm and the samadhi of prajna, you must cultivate the practice of prajna. Holding and reciting the Diamond Prajna Sutra, one sees the nature. You should know that the merit of this sutra is immeasurable and boundless; the sutra itself clearly praises it, and it cannot be fully spoken. This Dharma-gate is the supreme vehicle, spoken for the greatly wise, spoken for those of superior faculties; those of small wisdom and small faculties, hearing it, give rise to unbelief in their hearts.

Why? For example, when a dragon of heaven rains upon Jambudvipa, the cities and villages are all carried off, as the leaves of the jujube are swept along; but if it rains upon the great sea, it neither increases nor diminishes. If a man of the Great Vehicle, if a man of the supreme vehicle, hears the Diamond Sutra and his mind opens in understanding, he knows that the fundamental nature itself possesses prajna wisdom, and because he constantly contemplates with his own wisdom, he does not rely on words. For example, the rain does not come out of the sky itself; it is the dragon's power that stirs it up, that all sentient beings, all plants and trees, the sentient and the insentient alike, may all be moistened, while the hundred rivers and streams all flow into the great sea and become one body. The prajna wisdom of the fundamental nature of sentient beings is likewise.

Good friends! When those of small faculties hear this Sudden Teaching, it is like the plants and trees of small root: if caught in a great rain, they are all toppled over and cannot grow. Those of small faculties are likewise — though they originally have prajna wisdom with no difference from the greatly wise, why do they not awaken on hearing the Dharma? Because of the heavy obstruction of wrong views and the deep roots of affliction, like a great cloud covering the sun; without the wind to blow it away, the sunlight does not appear.

The wisdom of prajna has no great or small, because the self-minds of all beings differ in delusion and awakening. A deluded mind seeing outward, cultivating and seeking the Buddha, not yet awakened to the self-nature — this is small faculties. But if one is awakened to the Sudden Teaching, not holding to outward practice, and within one's own mind always raises right views, so that affliction and the dust of toil can never defile it — this is seeing the nature.

Good friends! Not dwelling within or without, going and coming freely, able to remove the clinging mind and penetrate without obstruction — one who cultivates this practice is in no way different from the Prajna Sutra.

Good friends! All sutras and all written texts — the two vehicles, the twelve divisions of the canon — are all established for people, depending on the nature of wisdom, and only then can they be set up. If there were no worldly people, all the myriad dharmas would originally not exist. Therefore know that the myriad dharmas are originally established by people, and all scriptures are spoken because of people. Because among people there are the dull and the wise, the dull are the small men and the wise the great men. The dull ask the wise, and the wise speak the Dharma for the dull; the dull, suddenly awakening, understanding and opening their minds, are no different from the wise.

Good friends! Without awakening, the Buddha is a sentient being; with a single thought of awakening, the sentient being is a Buddha. Therefore know that all the myriad dharmas are within your own mind — why not from your own mind suddenly see the true-tathata fundamental nature? The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Precepts says: "My own fundamental self-nature is pure; if you know your own mind and see the nature, all accomplish the Buddha-way." The Vimalakirti Sutra says: "Instantly it becomes all at once clear, and the original mind is regained."

Good friends! At the place of the Master Ren (Hongren), as soon as I heard a single phrase I awakened, and suddenly saw the true-tathata fundamental nature. Therefore I have spread this teaching abroad, so that those who study the Way may suddenly awaken to bodhi. Each of you contemplate your own mind and see your own fundamental nature.

If you cannot awaken yourselves, you must seek a great good friend, one who understands the Dharma of the supreme vehicle, to point directly to the right path. Such a good friend has a great relation — namely, to guide and transform so that one sees the nature; all good dharmas are able to be set moving because of the good friend. The Buddhas of the three times and the twelve divisions of the canon are originally complete within the nature of people. If one cannot awaken oneself, one must seek a good friend to point and show, and only then see; but if one awakens oneself, one need not seek outside. If one persists in holding that one must rely on a good friend outside and hopes to gain liberation thereby, there is no such principle. Why? Because within one's own mind there is a good friend who makes one aware and self-awakened. If one has given rise to wrong confusion and inverted, false thoughts, though an outward good friend can teach, he cannot save. But if one sets going the true, right prajna contemplation, in an instant all false thoughts are extinguished; if one recognizes the self-nature, in a single awakening one reaches the Buddha-ground.

Good friends! Contemplating with wisdom, within and without illumined and clear, one knows one's own fundamental mind. If you know the fundamental mind, you are fundamentally liberated. If you attain liberation, that is the samadhi of prajna, and that is "no-thought."

What is called no-thought? If, seeing all dharmas, the mind is not defiled by them, this is no-thought. In function it pervades every place, yet is not attached to any place. Only purify the fundamental mind, so that the six consciousnesses issue from the six gates, and amid the six objects there is no defilement and no mixing, going and coming freely, in universal function without obstruction — this is the samadhi of prajna, liberation at ease, called the practice of no-thought. If one thinks of nothing whatever, and causes thought to be cut off, that is Dharma-bondage, and is called a one-sided view.

Good friends! One who awakens to the no-thought Dharma penetrates all dharmas; one who awakens to the no-thought Dharma sees the realm of all Buddhas; one who awakens to the no-thought Dharma reaches the stage of Buddhahood.

Good friends! Among my descendants, those who obtain my Dharma, if they bring this Sudden Teaching gate, with those of like views and like practice, and make the vow to hold it as they would serve the Buddha, and to the end of life do not retreat — they will surely enter the sage's stage. But one must transmit the silent, secret transmission handed down from above, and must not conceal the right Dharma. If, with those of unlike views and unlike practice, in another teaching, one must not transmit it; for that would harm those former men, and in the end be of no benefit. I fear that the foolish, not understanding, might slander this Dharma-gate, and for a hundred eons and a thousand lives cut off the Buddha-seed nature.

Good friends! I have a "Verse of the Formless"; let each of you take it up and recite it, whether at home or in the monastery, and cultivate only in accord with it. If you do not cultivate yourselves and merely remember my words, it is of no benefit. Hear my verse:
Speech relates and mind relates, as the sun in the void abides; To pass on the seeing-nature Dharma, come forth and break the false guides.
The Dharma has no sudden or gradual; delusion and awakening have slow and fast. This gate of seeing the nature alone, the foolish cannot fully know.
Speech, though it is a thousand kinds, accords with principle and returns to one. In the dark house of affliction, one must ever raise the sun of wisdom.
When wrong comes, affliction arrives; when right comes, affliction is removed. Using neither wrong nor right, purity reaches the utterly without remainder.
Bodhi is the self-nature; to stir the mind is falsehood. The pure mind is amid falsehood; being right, there are no three hindrances.
If worldly people cultivate the Way, all things are no hindrance. Constantly seeing one's own faults, one is in accord with the Way.
Each class of form has its own Way, and they do not hinder or trouble one another. To leave the Way and seek another Way, to the end of life one will not see the Way.
Wave upon wave one passes a whole life, and in the end only regrets. If you would see the true Way, conduct that is upright is itself the Way.
If one has no mind for the Way, walking in darkness one does not see the Way. If one is a true cultivator of the Way, one does not see the faults of the world.
If you see the wrongs of others, your own wrong is the greater. Though another is wrong and I am not, when I am wrong I have a fault myself.
Only remove the mind of fault, and strike away affliction. Being unconcerned with hate and love, stretch out your two legs and lie down.
If you would transform others, you must yourself have expedient means. Do not let them have doubt; this is the self-nature revealing.
The Buddha-Dharma is in the world; it does not leave the worldly awakening. To seek bodhi apart from the world is exactly like seeking a rabbit's horn.
Right view is called transcendent; wrong view is called worldly. When wrong and right are both struck away, the bodhi nature is manifest.
This verse is the Sudden Teaching, also called the great Dharma-boat. The deluded hear it through many eons; the awakened in an instant.

The Master again said: Now, preaching this Sudden Teaching at the Great Brahma temple, I universally vow that sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, at these very words, see the nature and become Buddha.

At that time the Prefect Wei, with the officials and the clergy and lay alike, hearing what the Master said, none but awakened. All at once they made obeisance, and all lamented with joy, "Excellent! Who would have thought that in Lingnan a Buddha had appeared in the world!"

blocks.text: Third, the Chapter of Resolving Doubts

inline.s: One day the Prefect Wei held a great assembly feast for the Master. When the meal was done, the Prefect requested the Master to ascend the seat, and with the officials, scholars and commoners, of solemn countenance, made obeisance again and again, then asked, "Your disciple has heard the Master preach the Dharma, and it is truly inconceivable. Now I have a small doubt, and I beg the great compassion to explain it especially for me." The Master said, "If you have a doubt, ask at once; I will speak it for you."

The Prefect said, "What the Master preaches — is it not the fundamental implication of the Great Master Bodhidharma?" The Master said, "It is." The Prefect said, "Your disciple has heard that when Bodhidharma first taught Emperor Wu of Liang, the Emperor asked: 'I have all my life built temples, ordained monks, given alms and set up feasts; what merit have I gained?' Bodhidharma said: 'There is in truth no merit.' Your disciple has not yet penetrated this principle, and begs the Master to explain it."

The Master said: “Truly there is no merit! Do not doubt the words of the former sages. Emperor Wu’s mind was bent, and he did not know the true Dharma. Building monasteries, ordaining monks, giving alms, and setting up vegetarian feasts—these are called seeking blessings; one must not take blessings to be merit. Merit is within the Dharma-Body, and is not found in the cultivation of blessings.”

The Master again said: “To see the nature is merit, and to be equal is virtue. When every thought is unhindered and one constantly sees the true, wondrous function of one’s own nature, this is called merit. An inner mind that is humble is merit, and an outward conduct that accords with courtesy is virtue; the self-nature establishing all things is merit, and the mind-essence free from thoughts is virtue; never departing from the self-nature is merit, and applying it without defilement is virtue. If you would seek the merit and virtue of the Dharma-Body, simply practice according to this, and this is true merit and virtue.

One who cultivates merit never despises others but always practices universal respect. To be forever despising others, with the self never cut off—this is no merit of itself; one’s self-nature being vain and untrue—this is no virtue of itself. Because one makes the self great and always belittles everything.
Good friends! Unbroken thought is merit, and an upright and equal mind is virtue; cultivating the nature oneself is merit, and cultivating the body oneself is virtue.

Good friends! Merit and virtue must be seen within the self-nature; they are not something sought through almsgiving and offerings. Therefore blessing-virtue and merit-virtue are different. Emperor Wu did not know the truth—this is no fault of our Patriarch.”

The Prefect asked again: “Your disciple constantly sees monks and layfolk reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha and desiring rebirth in the West. I beg the Master to tell me whether they are reborn there, and to dispel my doubt.”

The Master said: “Listen well, Prefect! I will explain it to you. The World-Honored One, in the city of Śrāvastī, preached the scripture that guides beings to the West, making it clear that it is not far from here. But if one speaks of it in terms of distance by reckoning, there are one hundred and eight thousand [li] — that is, the ten evils and eight wrongs within one’s own body — which is to speak of it as far. To speak of it as far is for those of inferior faculties; to speak of it as near is for those of superior wisdom. There are two kinds of people, but the Dharma is not two; delusion and awakening differ, and seeing is swift or slow. The deluded person recites the Buddha’s name seeking rebirth there, while the awakened person purifies his own mind. Therefore the Buddha said: “When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.”

Prefect! A person of the East, only when his mind is pure, is without offense; even a person of the West, if his mind is impure, still has fault. A person of the East who commits offenses recites the Buddha’s name seeking rebirth in the West; a person of the West who commits offenses—in what land would he seek rebirth by reciting? The common and deluded do not understand the self-nature and do not recognize the Pure Land within their own bodies; they wish for the East or wish for the West, but to the awakened person it is the same wherever he is. Therefore the Buddha said: “Wherever one dwells, there is constant peace.” Prefect! If the ground of your mind is free of the not-good, the West is not far from here; but if you harbor a not-good mind, then however you recite the Buddha’s name it is hard to be reborn there.

Now I urge you good friends to first rid yourselves of the ten evils, and you will have traveled one hundred thousand [li]; then remove the eight wrongs, and you will have passed eight thousand. With every thought seeing the nature, always practicing what is upright and equal, you arrive as quickly as a snap of the fingers and behold Amitābha. Prefect! If you only practice the ten good deeds, what need is there to wish further for rebirth? If you do not cut off the mind of the ten evils, what Buddha will come to welcome you? If you awaken to the sudden Dharma of the unborn, you see the West in an instant; if you do not awaken, then reciting the Buddha’s name seeking rebirth—how can a path so distant be reached? I shall move the West before you in a single instant, and you shall see it right now—do you all wish to see it?”

The whole assembly bowed their heads and said: “If we can see it here, what need is there to wish further for rebirth? We beg the Master, in his compassion, to manifest the West at once, so that all may see it.”

The Master said: “Great assembly! The physical body of the world’s people is the city, and the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are the gates. Outside there are five gates, and within there is the gate of the mind. The mind is the ground, and the nature is the king; the king dwells upon the ground of the mind. When the nature is present the king is present, and when the nature departs the king is gone. When the nature is present the body and mind endure, and when the nature departs the body and mind are ruined. The Buddha is made within the nature—do not seek him outside the body. When the self-nature is deluded it is the sentient being, and when the self-nature is awakened it is the Buddha. Compassion is Avalokiteśvara, and joyous giving is called Mahāsthāmaprāpta; the one who can be pure is Śākyamuni, and uprightness is Amitābha. Self-and-other is Mount Sumeru, the deviant mind is the sea, affliction is the waves, cruelty is the evil dragon, falsehood is the ghosts and spirits, toil is the fish and turtles, greed and anger are the hells, and ignorance is the animals.

Good friends! Constantly practice the ten good deeds, and the heavenly palace will come; rid yourselves of self-and-other, and Sumeru falls; remove the deviant mind, and the sea dries up; when affliction is gone, the waves are stilled; when cruelty is removed, fish and dragons perish. When the nature of awareness, the Thus-Come-One, within the ground of your own mind, puts forth great light, it shines outwardly upon the six gates and makes them pure, able to break through the six desires of the heavens. When the self-nature shines within, the three poisons are at once removed, and the offenses of the hells and so forth are all destroyed in an instant. Within and without clear and bright, it is no different from the West. If you do not cultivate in this way, how can you reach that land?”

The great assembly, hearing this, clearly saw the nature, and all made obeisance, exclaiming together: “Well done!” and chanting: “We pray that all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm, upon hearing this, may be awakened at once.”

The Master said: “Good friends! If you wish to cultivate, it can be done while living at home; it is not necessary to be in a monastery. One who practices at home, like a person of the East whose mind is good, [is virtuous]; the one who does not cultivate in a monastery is like a person of the West whose mind is evil. Only when the mind is pure is this the self-nature’s Western Land.”

Master Wei asked again: “How does one cultivate while living at home? I beg you to instruct me.” The Master said: “I will speak to the assembly a ‘Verse on No-Form.’ If you cultivate according to it, you will always be no different from me. If you do not cultivate in this way, then even shaving your head and leaving home—what good is it to the Way? The verse says:
If the mind is at peace, why trouble to keep the precepts? If conduct is upright, what use to practice meditation?
Gratitude means personally nurturing father and mother; righteousness means loving high and low alike.
Yielding means harmony between high and low; forbearance means the many evils making no clamor.
If you can drill wood to draw forth fire, the red lotus is surely born from the mud.
What is bitter to the taste is good medicine; what grates upon the ear is sure to be loyal counsel.
Amending faults must beget wisdom; shielding one’s shortcomings is not virtue within.
In daily use always practice beneficence; attaining the Way is not by bestowing money.
Bodhi is only to be sought within the mind—why trouble to seek mystery outside!
Hear this, and if you cultivate according to it, the heavenly palace is only before your eyes.”

The Master again said: “Good friends! All of you must cultivate according to this verse, see your own nature, and directly accomplish the Buddha Way; the Dharma does not wait. Let everyone now disperse, for I shall return to Caoxi. If any of you have doubt, come and ask.”
At that time the Prefect, the officials, and the good men and faithful women gathered there, each attained awakening, believed, received, and practiced it.

blocks.text: 1. Concentration and Wisdom as the Foundation

inline.s: The Master instructed the assembly, saying: Good friends! In this Dharma-door of mine, concentration and wisdom are the foundation. Do not be deluded, great assembly, and say that concentration and wisdom are separate; they are one essence, not two. Concentration is the essence of wisdom, and wisdom is the function of concentration. At the very moment of wisdom, concentration is in wisdom; at the very moment of concentration, wisdom is in concentration. If you understand this meaning, then you study concentration and wisdom equally.

All you who study the Way! Do not say, “First concentration produces wisdom, first wisdom produces concentration,” as though they were each distinct. One who holds this view sees the Dharma as having two aspects. One who speaks good words with a mind that is not good, having only empty concentration and wisdom, [makes] concentration and wisdom unequal; but if mind and mouth are both good, within and without as one, then concentration and wisdom are equal. Self-awakening and self-cultivation do not lie in disputation; if one disputes what comes first, he is the same as the deluded. Not cutting off victory and defeat only increases self and Dharma, and does not depart from the four marks.

Good friends! To what is concentration and wisdom likened? They are like a lamp and its light. With the lamp there is light, and without the lamp it is dark; the lamp is the essence of the light, and the light is the function of the lamp. Though their names are two, their essence is originally one. This Dharma of concentration and wisdom is just the same.

The Master instructed the assembly, saying: Good friends! The single-practice samādhi is this: in all places, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, always practice the single upright mind. As the ‘Vimalakīrti Sutra’ says: “The upright mind is the place of practice; the upright mind is the Pure Land.” Do not let the mind practice flattery and crookedness while the mouth only speaks of uprightness, saying ‘single-practice samādhi’ and yet not practicing the upright mind. Only practice the upright mind, and in all things do not cling. The deluded cling to Dharmamarks and grasp at the single-practice samādhi, declaring outright: “To sit constantly without moving, with false thoughts not arising in the mind—this is the single-practice samādhi.” One who understands it thus is the same as an insentient thing; this is precisely a cause that obstructs the Way.

Good friends! The Way must flow freely—why does it get stuck? When the mind does not abide in things, the Way flows freely; if the mind abides in things, that is called binding oneself. If one says that sitting constantly without moving is right, it is only like Śāriputra sitting quietly in the forest, yet he was reproached by Vimalakīrti.

Good friends! There are others who teach people to sit, watching the mind and contemplating stillness, not moving and not arising, and from this setting up their effort. The deluded do not understand, and grasp at this until it becomes a derangement—such people are many. Teaching one another in this way, one knows this is a great error!

The Master instructed the assembly, saying: Good friends! The true teaching is originally without sudden or gradual, but the natures of people are themselves sharp or dull. The deluded cultivate gradually, while the awakened awaken suddenly. If one knows his own mind and sees his own nature, there is no difference. Therefore it is only the provisional name of sudden and gradual.

Good friends! In this Dharma-door of mine, from the beginning it has established no-thought as the doctrine, no-form as the essence, and no-abiding as the foundation. No-form means being free of form amid forms. No-thought means being without thought amid thought. No-abiding is the original nature of people: amid the good and evil, beautiful and ugly of the world, even amid enemies and kin, when words and speech stab and provoke and deceive and contend, all is taken as empty, with no thought of requital or harm, and within thought there is no dwelling on past conditions. If past thought, present thought, and future thought succeed one another without break, that is called bondage; but when in all things thought does not abide, then there is no bondage. This is taking no-abiding as the foundation.
Good friends! To be free of all marks externally is called no-form. Able to be free of marks, the Dharma-essence is pure. This is taking no-form as the essence.

Good friends! When the mind is unstained amidst all objects, this is called no-thought. On one’s own thought always be free of objects, and do not give rise to mind upon objects. If one simply thinks of nothing and cuts off all thought, then the moment thought ceases it is death, and one is reborn elsewhere—this is a great error. You who study the Way, consider this! If you do not understand the meaning of the Dharma, your own error may be excused, but to encourage others besides—being confused and unable to see for oneself, and moreover slandering the Buddha’s scriptures—therefore no-thought is established as the doctrine.

Good friends! Why is no-thought established as the doctrine? Only because one merely says with the mouth that he sees the nature, while the deluded, having thought upon objects, give rise to wrong views upon that thought, and from this all toil and false imaginings are born. The self-nature is originally without a single thing to be attained; if there is anything attained, and one vainly speaks of fortune and misfortune, that is toil and wrong view. Therefore this Dharma-door establishes no-thought as the doctrine.

Good friends! What is ‘no’, and what is ‘thought’? No means no duality and no mind of toil; thought means thinking the original nature of suchness. Suchness is the essence of thought, and thought is the function of suchness. The self-nature of suchness gives rise to thought; it is not the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue that can think. Suchness has a nature, therefore thought arises. If suchness did not exist, eyes, ears, sound, and form would be ruined at once.

Good friends! When the self-nature of suchness gives rise to thought, although the six faculties have seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, they are unstained by the myriad objects, and the true nature is always self-possessed. Therefore the scripture says: “Able to distinguish well the marks of all things, yet unmoved in the supreme meaning.”

The Master instructed the assembly, saying: In this door, sitting meditation is originally not to fix the mind, nor to fix purity, nor is it the unmoving [body]. If one says fix the mind, the mind is originally false; knowing the mind is like an illusion, therefore there is nothing fixed. If one says fix purity, the nature of people is originally pure, but because of false thoughts it is covered, concealing suchness; if only there are no false thoughts, the nature is of itself pure. To set the mind on purity gives rise to the falsehood of purity; falsehood has no place, and what is fixed is false. Purity has no form, yet one sets up a mark of purity and calls it practice! One who holds this view obstructs his own nature and is bound by purity.

Good friends! One who practices unmovingness, when seeing every person, sees not the person’s right and wrong, good and evil, and faults—this is the self-nature unmoved. Good friends! The deluded person, though his body does not move, opens his mouth and speaks of the right and wrong, the merits and faults, the likes and dislikes of others—this is contrary to the Way. To fix the mind and to fix purity is to obstruct the Way.

The Master instructed the assembly, saying: Good friends! What is called sitting meditation? In this Dharma-door, without obstruction and without hindrance, when externally no thought arises in the mind amid all good and evil realms, that is called sitting; and then internally seeing the self-nature unmoved is called meditation.

Good friends! What is called meditative concentration? When externally free of marks is meditation, and internally unconfused is concentration. If externally one is attached to marks, the inner mind is at once confused; if externally one is free of marks, the mind is at once unconfused. The original nature is of itself pure and of itself concentrated; it is only because one sees objects and thinks of objects that it becomes confused. If one sees the various objects and the mind remains unconfused, that is true concentration.

Good friends! Externally free of marks is meditation, and internally unconfused is concentration; external meditation and internal concentration—this is meditative concentration. The ‘Bodhisattva Precept Sutra’ says: “My original self-nature is pure.” Good friends! In every thought, see the self-nature pure, cultivate it yourself and practice it yourself, and accomplish the Buddha Way yourself.

blocks.text: 1. Transmitting the Incense of the Dharma-Body

inline.s: At that time the Great Master saw the people of Guangzhou and Shaozhou and the scholars and common folk from the four quarters gathering in the mountain to hear the Dharma, so he ascended the seat and told the assembly: Come! All you good friends! This matter must arise from within the self-nature. At all times, in every thought, purify your own mind, cultivate and practice yourself, see your own Dharma-Body, see your own mind-Buddha, save yourself and discipline yourself, and only then have you not come in vain. Since you have come from afar and gathered here in one assembly, you all share the same affinity. Now each of you may place your knees upon the ground, and first I will transmit the incense of the five-part Dharma-Body of the self-nature, and next bestow the formless repentance.
The assembly bowed with knees upon the ground. The Master said:
1. The incense of precepts. That in one’s own mind there is no wrong, no evil, no jealousy, no greed or anger, no harm—this is called the incense of precepts.
2. The incense of concentration. Beholding the marks of good and evil realms, one’s own mind is not confused—this is called the incense of concentration.

3. The incense of wisdom. One’s own mind unhindered, constantly using wisdom to contemplate the self-nature, doing no evil, and though practicing all good, not clinging with the mind, respecting those above and caring for those below, compassionate to the orphaned and the poor—this is called the incense of wisdom.
4. The incense of liberation. That one’s own mind grasps at nothing, thinks not of good and not of evil, at ease and unhindered—this is called the incense of liberation.

5. The incense of liberation’s knowledge and vision. Since one’s own mind grasps at neither good nor evil, one must not sink into emptiness and rest in stillness, but should learn widely and hear much, know one’s own original mind, reach the principles of the Buddhas, harmonize one’s light and approach all beings, without self and without others, until one attains the true nature of bodhi which does not change—this is called the incense of liberation’s knowledge and vision.
Good friends! This incense each of you should kindle within yourself—do not seek it outside.

Now I shall bestow upon you the formless repentance, to extinguish the offenses of the three times and to make the three karmas pure. Good friends! Follow my words each of you, and say together at once:

We disciples, in past thought, present thought, and future thought, in every thought, are not stained by ignorance and delusion; all the evil karma of ignorance and delusion and such offenses from the past, we all repent, praying that they may be destroyed at once and never arise again.

We disciples, in past thought, present thought, and future thought, in every thought, are not stained by pride and deceit; all the evil karma of pride and deceit and such offenses from the past, we all repent, praying that they may be destroyed at once and never arise again.

We disciples, in past thought, present thought, and future thought, in every thought, are not stained by jealousy; all the evil karma of jealousy and such offenses from the past, we all repent, praying that they may be destroyed at once and never arise again.

Good friends! What has gone before is the formless repentance. What is called ‘repent’, and what is called ‘regret’? Repent means repenting of one’s former faults; all the evil karma of ignorance and delusion, pride and deceit, jealousy and such offenses from the past, is utterly repented, never to arise again—this is called repent. Regret means regretting one’s later faults; from now onward all evil karma of ignorance and delusion, pride and deceit, jealousy and such offenses, now that one is awakened, is utterly and forever cut off, never to be done again—this is called regret. Therefore it is called repentance. The common and deluded only know how to repent of their former faults and do not know how to regret their later faults. Because they do not regret, the former faults are not extinguished and the later faults arise again. If the former faults are not extinguished and the later faults continue to arise, what is repentance?
Good friends! Having repented, I will now, together with you good friends, make the Four Great Vows; each of you must listen with all your mind:
The sentient beings of my own mind, boundless as they are, I vow to save them all;
The afflictions of my own mind, endless as they are, I vow to cut them off;
The Dharma-doors of my own nature, measureless as they are, I vow to study them all;
The Buddha Way of my own nature, unsurpassed as it is, I vow to accomplish it.

Good friends! Do you not all say ‘the sentient beings, boundless as they are, I vow to save them all’? Though you say this, it is not that Huineng saves them. Good friends! The sentient beings within the mind—what are called the mind of wrong views, the mind of deception, the mind of unwholesomeness, the mind of jealousy, the mind of malice, and such minds—these are all sentient beings; each one must save himself by his own self-nature, and this is called true salvation.

What is called saving oneself by one’s own self-nature? It is saving the sentient beings of wrong views, afflictions, and ignorance in one’s own mind with right views. Having right views, use the wisdom of prajñā to break through the ignorant, deluded, and false sentient beings, each saving himself. When wrong comes, right saves it; when delusion comes, awakening saves it; when ignorance comes, wisdom saves it; when evil comes, good saves it—this kind of salvation is called true salvation.
Again, ‘the afflictions, endless as they are, I vow to cut them off’: it is to use the wisdom of prajñā of the self-nature to rid oneself of the mind of false thinking.
Again, ‘the Dharma-doors, measureless as they are, I vow to study them all’: one must see one’s own nature and constantly practice the true Dharma—this is called true study.

Again, ‘the Buddha Way, unsurpassed as it is, I vow to accomplish it’: if one can always humble the mind, practice what is genuine and upright, be free of delusion and free of awakening, always give rise to prajñā, remove the true and remove the false, then one sees the Buddha-nature, and at once, upon these words, accomplishes the Buddha Way.
Always remember: cultivation is a matter of the power of vows.

blocks.text: 4. The Precepts of the Three Refuges

inline.s: Good friends! Now that you have made the Four Great Vows, I will further bestow upon you good friends the formless precepts of the Three Refuges. Good friends!
Take refuge in Awareness, the honored one who is complete in both [merit and wisdom];
Take refuge in Uprightness, the honored one who is free of desire;
Take refuge in Purity, the honored one among the assembly.

From today onward, call Awareness your teacher, and no longer take refuge in the wrong demons and outside paths; and so have the Three Jewels of the self-nature constantly testify to it. I urge you good friends to take refuge in the Three Jewels of the self-nature: the Buddha is awareness, the Dharma is uprightness, and the Sangha is purity.

When the mind takes refuge in Awareness, wrong delusion does not arise, desire is reduced and contentment known, and one can be free of wealth and lust—this is called the honored one complete in both. When the mind takes refuge in Uprightness, every thought is without wrong view; because of no wrong view, there is no self-and-other pride or greed and clinging—this is called the honored one free of desire. When the mind takes refuge in Purity, amid all realms of toil, love, and desire the self-nature is wholly unstained—this is called the honored one among the assembly.

If one practices in this way, that is taking refuge oneself. The ordinary person who does not understand, from day to night, receives the precepts of the Three Refuges [only outwardly]. If one says take refuge in the Buddha, where is the Buddha? If one does not see the Buddha, on what does one rely? Such words become false.

Good friends! Each of you observe carefully and do not misdirect your mind. The scripture plainly says to take refuge in the Buddha of oneself, and not to take refuge in another Buddha. If one does not take refuge in one’s own Buddha, there is no place to rely upon. Now that you have awakened, each must take refuge in the Three Jewels of one’s own mind: within, harmonize the mind-nature; without, respect others—this is taking refuge oneself.

blocks.text: 5. The One Essence and Three Bodies

inline.s: Good friends! Having completed taking refuge in the Three Jewels of oneself, each of you set your mind and I will speak to you of the One Essence and Three Bodies as the self-nature Buddha, so that you may see the three bodies and clearly awaken of yourselves to the self-nature. Follow all my words: upon your own physical body take refuge in the pure Dharma-Body Buddha; upon your own physical body take refuge in the complete Reward-Body Buddha; upon your own physical body take refuge in the hundred-thousand-million Transformation-Body Buddha.

Good friends! The physical body is but a dwelling and cannot be spoken of as [something to take refuge in]. The three-body Buddha of which I have just spoken is within the self-nature, and everyone has it. Because the mind is deluded and does not see the inner nature, they seek the three-body Thus-Come-One outside and do not see the three-body Buddha within their own bodies. You have heard me say this so that you may see within your own bodies the self-nature possessing the three-body Buddha. These three-body Buddhas are born of the self-nature and are not attained from outside.

What is called the pure Dharma-Body Buddha? The nature of people is originally pure, and all things are born from the self-nature. If one reflects on all evil matters, evil conduct arises; if one reflects on all good matters, good conduct arises. Thus all things are within the self-nature, as the sky is always clear and the sun and moon always bright; when covered by floating clouds, above is bright and below is dark, but when a wind suddenly blows the clouds away, above and below are both bright and the ten thousand images all appear. The nature of people is always drifting about, like those clouds of the sky. Good friends! Wisdom is like the sun and prajñā is like the moon; wisdom and prajñā are always bright. When attached to objects without, the self-nature is covered by the floating clouds of false thought and cannot be clear. If one meets a good friend and hears the true Dharma, one removes delusion and falsehood oneself, and within and without is clear and bright, and within the self-nature all things appear. One who sees the nature is also thus. This is called the pure Dharma-Body Buddha.

Good friends! When the mind takes refuge in the self-nature, it is taking refuge in the true Buddha. Taking refuge oneself means removing from the self-nature the mind of unwholesomeness, the mind of jealousy, the mind of flattery, the mind of self-and-other, the mind of deception, the mind of despising others, the mind of arrogance toward others, the mind of wrong views, the mind of pride, and all unwholesome conduct at all times; always see one’s own faults and do not speak of the good or bad of others—this is taking refuge oneself. Always humble the mind and universally practice reverence; this is seeing the nature and passing through freely, with no more obstruction—this is taking refuge oneself.

What is called the complete Reward-Body Buddha? For example, a single lamp can dispel a thousand years of darkness, and a single thought of wisdom can destroy ten thousand years of ignorance. Do not ponder the past, for what has passed cannot be recovered; always think of what is to come, and in every thought be perfectly bright, seeing one’s own nature. Though good and evil differ, the original nature is nondual; the nature that is nondual is called the true nature. Within the true nature, unstained by good or evil, this is called the complete Reward-Body Buddha. When the self-nature gives rise to a single thought of evil, it destroys the good causes of ten thousand kalpas; when the self-nature gives rise to a single thought of good, it exhausts evil as countless as the sands of the Ganges. Until supreme bodhi, in every thought see for yourself, never losing the original thought—this is called the Reward-Body.

What is called the hundred-thousand-million Transformation-Body Buddha? If one does not think of the myriad things, the nature is as empty of itself. A single thought of reflection is called transformation. Reflecting on evil matters, it transforms into the hells; reflecting on good matters, it transforms into the heavens; cruelty transforms into dragons and serpents; compassion transforms into bodhisattvas; wisdom transforms into the upper realms; ignorance transforms into the lower regions. The self-nature transforms very much, but the deluded cannot be aware of it. When every thought gives rise to evil, one constantly walks the evil paths; turn back to a single thought of good, and wisdom is at once born. This is called the Transformation-Body Buddha of the self-nature.

Good friends! The Dharma-Body is originally complete; in every thought, seeing the self-nature oneself, that is the Reward-Body Buddha; reflecting from the Reward-Body, that is the Transformation-Body Buddha. To awaken oneself, cultivate oneself, and accomplish the merit of the self-nature is true taking of refuge. Skin and flesh are the physical body, and the physical body is the dwelling, of which one does not speak of taking refuge. Only awaken to the self-nature’s three bodies, and you will know the self-nature Buddha.
I have a ‘Verse on No-Form’; if you can recite it and hold it, upon these words it will make the deluded offenses accumulated over kalpas vanish in an instant. The verse says:
The deluded cultivate blessings and do not cultivate the Way, thinking only that cultivating blessings is the Way;
Almsgiving and offerings bring blessings without limit, but the three evils in the mind were originally the makers [of them].
Meaning to use the cultivation of blessings to extinguish offenses, in a later life one gains blessings and the offenses remain;
Only remove from within the mind the causes of offense, and in each self-nature is true repentance.
Suddenly awakening to the true repentance of the Great Vehicle, removing wrong and practicing right, one is without offense;
One who studies the Way constantly contemplates the self-nature, and is of the same kind as all the Buddhas.
Our Patriarchs transmitted only this sudden Dharma, universally hoping that seeing the nature is one same essence;
If in the future you would seek the Dharma-Body, be free of the marks of all things and wash the mind within.
Strive to see for yourself, do not linger; when a future thought is suddenly cut off, this life is over;
If you awaken to the Great Vehicle and see the nature, reverently fold your hands and seek with your whole heart.

The Master said: Good friends! All of you must recite it and cultivate according to it; upon these words you will see the nature, and though you be a thousand li from me, it is as though you were always at my side. If upon these words you do not awaken, then though you be face to face a thousand li away, how does your coming from far avail you? Take care, and go well!
The whole assembly, hearing the Dharma, was all awakened, and joyfully practiced it.

After receiving the Dharma at Huangmei, the Master returned to Caohou Village in Shaozhou, and no one knew who he was. There was a Confucian scholar Liu Zhilüe, who treated him with great courtesy. Zhilüe had an aunt who was a nun, named Wujinzang, who constantly recited the ‘Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra.’ The Master, hearing her recite but briefly, at once knew its subtle meaning, and explained it to her. The nun then took up the scroll and asked him about characters. The Master said: “I do not recognize characters; if you ask about the meaning, please ask.” The nun said: “If you do not even recognize characters, how can you understand the meaning?” The Master said: “The subtle principle of all Buddhas is not a matter of words.” The nun was astonished at this, and told all the elders of the village: “This is a man of the Way; you should invite and support him.” There was also Cao Shuliang, a descendant of Marquis Wei Wu, together with the villagers, who came one after another to pay their respects.

At that time the ancient Baolin Monastery had been ruined by the fires of war at the end of the Sui, and so upon its old foundations they rebuilt the temple and invited the Master to dwell there, and before long it became a jewel of a place. The Master lived there for more than nine months, and then was again pursued by an evil faction. The Master then withdrew
(same as “recede”)

to the front mountain, where they set fire to the grass and trees, and the Master hid himself, pressing into a rock, and so escaped. On that rock there are still the knee-prints of the Master’s cross-legged sitting and the pattern of his robe, and so it is called the Refuge-from-Peril Rock. Remembering the instruction of the Fifth Patriarch “to hide for a while at Huai-Hui,” the Master went and hid himself in those two districts.

blocks.text: 2. This Very Mind Is the Buddha

inline.s: The monk Fahai, a man of Qujiang in Shaozhou, came to the Patriarch for instruction and asked: “This very mind is the Buddha—I beg you to point this out.” The Master said: “When the previous thought does not arise, that is the mind; when the later thought is not extinguished, that is the Buddha. Forming all marks is the mind, and being free of all marks is the Buddha. If I were to speak of it fully, it could not be exhausted in a whole kalpa. Hear my verse:
“The mind is called wisdom, and the Buddha is concentration;
Concentration and wisdom held in equal measure, the mind is pure within.
If you awaken to this Dharma-door, it is by your own practice;
Its function is originally unborn; to cultivate both is the right way.”
Fahai, upon these words, was greatly awakened, and praised it in a verse:
“This mind is originally the Buddha; not awakening, one wrongs oneself;
I know the cause of concentration and wisdom—cultivating both, one is free of all things.”

blocks.text: 3. The Head Not Touching the Ground

inline.s: The monk Fada, a man of Hongzhou, left home at seven and constantly recited the ‘Lotus Sutra.’ He came to bow to the Patriarch, but his head did not touch the ground. The Patriarch reproached him, saying: “If in bowing you do not bow to the ground, how is it better than not bowing at all! There must be something in your mind—what is it you have been nurturing?” He said: “I have recited the ‘Lotus Sutra’ and have reached three thousand [copies].” The Master said: “If you recited it to ten thousand copies, and grasped the meaning of the sutra, and did not take that as an accomplishment, then you would travel together with me. Now you are burdened with this [task] and do not even know your fault! Hear my verse:
“Ritual is meant to break the banner of pride—why does your head not touch the ground?
With a self, offense is born; forgetting accomplishment, blessings are incomparable.”
The Master again said: “What is your name?” He said: “My name is Fada.” The Master said: “You are named Fada [Reaching the Dharma] — have you ever reached the Dharma?” And he further spoke a verse:
“Now your name is Fada, diligently reciting without rest;
Reciting emptily, only following the sound; one who illumines the mind is called a bodhisattva.
Now you have an affinity, and I now speak for you;
Only believe that the Buddha is wordless, and the lotus flower issues from the mouth.”

Fada, hearing the verse, repented and thanked him, saying: “From now on I shall be humble and respectful to all. Your disciple has recited the ‘Lotus Sutra’ but has not understood its meaning, and my mind is ever full of doubt. The Master’s wisdom is vast—I beg you to explain briefly the meaning within the sutra.”

blocks.text: 4. The Meaning of the Lotus Sutra

inline.s: The Master said: “Fada! The Dharma is wholly reached, but your mind has not reached it. The sutra is originally without doubt, but your mind doubts itself. You recite this sutra—what do you take as its doctrine?” Fada said: “Your student’s faculties are dull, and from the beginning I have only recited the text; how would I know its doctrine?” The Master said: “I do not recognize characters; you try reading the sutra aloud once, and I shall explain it for you.”

Fada then recited the sutra aloud, and when he reached the ‘Chapter on Parables,’ the Master said: “Stop! This sutra has from the beginning taken the cause and condition of appearing in the world as its doctrine. Even speaking many kinds of parables, it does not go beyond this. What is this cause and condition? The sutra says: ‘The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, only for the one great cause and condition appear in the world.’ This one great matter is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The people of the world are outwardly deluded and attached to marks, and inwardly deluded and attached to emptiness. If they can be free of marks amid marks and free of emptiness amid emptiness, then within and without they are not deluded. If you awaken to this Dharma, the mind opens in a single thought—this is opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The Buddha is, as it were, awareness, divided into four gates: opening the knowledge and vision of awareness, showing the knowledge and vision of awareness, awakening to the knowledge and vision of awareness, and entering the knowledge and vision of awareness. If, upon hearing the opening and showing, one can awaken and enter, this is the knowledge and vision of awareness, whereby the original true nature appears. Do not be careless and mistake the meaning of the sutra!
