When you see others speak of opening, showing, awakening, and entering, [know that] this is the knowledge and vision of the Buddha, and that we have no share in it. If you understand it thus, you are slandering the sutra and reviling the Buddha. Since it is the Buddha, he already possesses the knowledge and vision—why need it be opened? Now you should believe this: the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is only your own mind, and there is no other Buddha.

It is because all sentient beings, obscuring their own brightness, crave the dusty realms, and troubled within while bound to conditions without, willingly run about, that the World-Honored One, compassionately rousing himself from samādhi, spoke with all manner of bitter words, urging them to be still. Do not seek outside; [your nature] is not other than the Buddha’s. Therefore it is said to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

I too urge all people, within their own minds, constantly to open the Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision. People of the world, with skewed hearts, deluded and ignorant, create offenses: they speak well but act evilly — greedy, angry, jealous, fawning, and proud; encroaching on others and harming things, they open the beings-knowledge. If one can rectify the mind, constantly give rise to wisdom, contemplatively illuminate one's own mind, cease evil and practice good, this is to open the Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision.

You must, thought after thought, open the Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision; do not open the beings-knowledge. To open the Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision is to transcend the world; to open the beings-knowledge is to remain in the world. If you merely toil and cling to thoughts, taking that as your practice, how is this different from a yak that loves its own tail?”

blocks.text: 5. Reciting with the Mouth, Practicing with the Mind

inline.s: Fada said, "If that is so, then one need only grasp the meaning and need not trouble to recite the sutra?" The Master said, "What fault has the sutra, that it should hinder your mindfulness? It is only that delusion and awakening lie in the person, and benefit and harm in oneself. To recite with the mouth while practicing with the mind is to turn the sutra; to recite with the mouth while not practicing with the mind is to be turned by the sutra. Hear my verse:"
The mind deluded is turned by the Lotus; the mind awakened turns the Lotus;
reciting the sutra long without understanding, one makes an enemy of its meaning.
To be without thought in thought is right; to be with thought in thought is wrong;
counting neither the having nor the void, ever one rides the great white bullock cart.”

Fada heard the verse and, without knowing it, wept; in these words he was greatly enlightened, and said to the Master, "Fada, from former times, has never actually turned the Lotus Sutra; rather he was turned by the Lotus Sutra."

He again opened his lips, saying, "The sutra says that the great sravakas and even the bodhisattvas “exhaust their thought and measure together, yet cannot fathom the Buddha's wisdom.” Now, if you tell an ordinary person that merely to awaken to his own mind is called the Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision, then one who is not of superior faculties will inevitably doubt and slander. Also, the sutra speaks of three carts, the goat, the stag, and the bullock, how do these differ from the great white bullock cart? I pray the Master again condescend to instruct me."

The Master said, "The meaning of the sutra is clear; you are yourself deluded and turned against it. That those in the three vehicles cannot fathom the Buddha's wisdom is due to the fault of measuring and reckoning. Even if they exhaust thought and join their reasoning, they set it only farther away. The Buddha originally spoke for ordinary beings, not for the Buddha. If a person will not believe this principle, let him withdraw from the assembly."

Little do they know that, seated as they are in the great white bullock cart, they go outside the gate in search of the three carts. Moreover, the text of the sutra clearly tells you, "There is only the single Buddha vehicle, and no other vehicle. Whether two or three, even countless expedient means, the manifold causes and conditions, parables and words, all these dharmas are for the sake of the single Buddha vehicle." Why do you not consider this?

The three carts are provisional, for the sake of earlier times; the single vehicle is real, for the sake of the present time. It only teaches you to leave the provisional and return to the real; and once returned to the real, even the real has no name. You should know that all the treasure belongs entirely to you and is for your use, so that you no longer think of a father, nor think of a son, nor think of using anything. This is called upholding the Lotus Sutra: from kalpa to kalpa never letting go of the scroll, from dawn to dusk never without the time of mindfulness.”
Fada, awakened by this, leapt for joy and praised it in a verse:
Reciting three thousand scrolls, at a single phrase of Caoxi it vanished;
without the aim of transcending the world, how could the wildness of many lives be stilled?
The goat, the stag, and the bullock are expediently set; the good is spoken in the early, middle, and later times;
who knows that within the burning house there was, from the first, a king of the Dharma.”
The Master said, "From now on you may be called a monk who recites the sutra." From that time on Fada grasped the mysterious aim, and yet never ceased reciting the sutra.

blocks.text: 7. The Three Bodies and the Four Wisdoms

inline.s: The monk Zhitong was a native of Anfeng in Shouzhou. At first he studied the Lankavatara Sutra through about a thousand or more recitations, yet could not understand the three bodies and four wisdoms, so he bowed to the Master and asked him to explain their meaning. The Master said, "The three bodies: the pure Dharmakaya is your own nature; the complete Sambhogakaya is your own wisdom; the hundred, thousand, and myriads of transformation bodies are your own action. If, apart from the original nature, you speak of three bodies separately, that is called having bodies without wisdom. If you awaken that the three bodies have no self-nature, that is called the four wisdoms of bodhi. Hear my verse:"
The self-nature is endowed with the three bodies, and when revealed becomes the four wisdoms;
without departing from the conditions of seeing and hearing, one transcends to the ground of Buddhahood.
I now tell this to you; believe it truly and never be deluded;
do not imitate those who run about seeking, who talk of bodhi all day long.”

Tong again asked, "May I hear the meaning of the four wisdoms?" The Master said, "Since you have understood the three bodies, you will then be clear about the four wisdoms, why ask again? If, apart from the three bodies, you separately speak of the four wisdoms, this is called having wisdom without bodies; and that very wisdom becomes no wisdom." Then he gave a verse
The great mirror-wisdom is of pure nature; the equality-wisdom has a mind free of disease,
the wondrous observing-wisdom sees without a trace of effort; the truth-accomplishing-wisdom is like the perfect mirror.
The fifth, eighth, sixth, and seventh are turned in fruit and cause; only names and words are used, and there is no real nature;
if at the turning you leave no trace of feeling, amid the many arisings you forever dwell in the naga samadhi.

As above, the consciousnesses are turned into wisdoms. The teaching says: "Turn the first five consciousnesses into the truth-accomplishing-wisdom; turn the sixth into the wondrous observing-wisdom; turn the seventh into the equality-wisdom; turn the eighth into the great mirror-wisdom." Though the sixth and seventh are turned in the cause and the fifth and eighth in the fruit, only their names are turned, not their substance.”
Tong suddenly awakened to the nature-wisdom, and offered a verse:
The three bodies are my primal body; the four wisdoms are the mind's native brightness,
body and wisdom merge without obstacle; responding to things, freely following every form.
To rise up and cultivate is all false stirring; to hold fast and guard is not the true essence,
the subtle aim was made known by the Master; in the end, the name of defilement is gone.”

blocks.text: 8. The Original Mind and the Original Nature

inline.s: The monk Zhichang was a native of Guixi in Xinzhou; he left the household life in childhood, resolved to see his nature. One day he came to pay his respects, and the Master asked, "Whence have you come, and what do you seek?" He said, "Your student recently went to Mount Baifeng in Hongzhou to pay respects to the monk Datong, and was shown the meaning of seeing nature and becoming Buddha. But my fox-like doubt is not yet settled, so I have come from afar to bow to you. I humbly beg the Master, in compassion, to instruct me." The Master said, "What words did he speak? Try to present them and let me see."

He said, "When Zhichang arrived there, three months passed without my receiving instruction. Because I was so earnest for the Dharma, one night I went alone into the abbot's room and asked, 'What is this person's original mind and original nature?' Datong then said, 'Do you see the sky?' I answered, 'I do.' He said, 'Do you see any form or feature in the sky?' I answered, 'The sky is formless; what feature could it have?' He said, 'Your original nature is like the sky: not a single thing is seen in it, and this is called right seeing; not a single thing is known in it, and this is called true knowledge. Free of blue and yellow, long and short, seeing only that the original source is pure and the body of awakening is round and bright, this is called seeing nature and becoming Buddha, and is also called the Tathagata's knowledge and vision.' Though your student heard this, he still could not settle it, and begs the Master to instruct him."
The Master said, "What that teacher spoke still retained a view-and-knowledge, and so made you unable to settle it. I will now show you a verse:"
To see no dharma and hold a view of nothing, is most like a drifting cloud veiling the sun's face;
to know no dharma and hold a void knowledge, is still like the great space giving birth to a flash of lightning.
When this view-and-knowledge arises in a glance, and is mistaken, how can one understand the expedient means?
You should, in a single thought, know your own fault, and your own spirit-light will ever shine forth.”
Zhichang heard the verse and his mind opened at once; he then set forth a verse:
Without a cause one rouses view-and-knowledge, and clinging to marks seeks bodhi;
if feeling retains so much as a single thought of awakening, how can it surpass the earlier delusion?
The self-nature is the source of awakening; following the illumination, in vain it drifts and flows;
unless one enters the patriarch's chamber, confusedly one runs toward the two extremes.”

One day Zhichang asked the Master, "The Buddha spoke of the three vehicles, and again spoke of the supreme vehicle; your disciple does not understand, and begs you to teach him." The Master said, "Observe your own original mind; do not fix upon the marks of external dharmas. The Dharma has no four vehicles; it is the minds of people that differ. Delighting in seeing, hearing, and reciting is the small vehicle; awakening to the Dharma and understanding its meaning is the middle vehicle; practicing in accord with the Dharma is the great vehicle. To pass through all dharmas, to possess all dharmas, unstained by anything, to depart from all marks of dharmas, with not a single thing attained, this is called the supreme vehicle. The vehicle is a matter of practice, not of contention in words. You must cultivate it yourself; do not ask me. In all times the self-nature is as it is." Zhichang bowed in thanks, waited upon the Master, and served him to the end of his life.

The monk Zhidao was a native of Nanhai in Guangzhou. Seeking instruction, he said, "Since leaving the household life, your student has read the Nirvana Sutra for more than ten years without understanding its main import. I pray the Master condescend to teach me." The Master said, "Where is it that you do not understand?" He said, "“All formations are impermanent; this is the law of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing are extinguished, still extinction is bliss.” Here I am in doubt."

The Master said, "How is it that you doubt?" He said, "All sentient beings have two bodies: the physical body and the Dharmakaya. The physical body is impermanent, arising and ceasing; the Dharmakaya is eternal, without knowledge or feeling. The sutra says, “When arising and ceasing are extinguished, still extinction is bliss.” I do not know which body is extinguished, and which body experiences bliss. If it is the physical body, then when the physical body ceases, the four great elements disperse, and it is wholly suffering; where there is suffering, one cannot speak of bliss. If it is the Dharmakaya that is extinguished, it would be the same as grass, trees, tiles, and stones, who then experiences bliss? Moreover, dharmanature is the substance of arising and ceasing, and the five aggregates are the function of arising and ceasing; one substance with five functions, so arising and ceasing are eternal. When there is arising, the function rises from the substance; when there is ceasing, the function is gathered back into the substance. If regeneration is allowed, then sentient beings are never cut off and never extinguished; if regeneration is not allowed, then all is eternally returned to stillness, the same as insentient things. If this is so, then all dharmas are restrained and subdued by nirvana and cannot even arise, what bliss is there?"

The Master said, "You are a son of the Buddha; why do you study the heretical views of annihilation and eternalism, and discuss the supreme vehicle? According to what you say, there is a Dharmakaya apart from the physical body, and you seek still extinction apart from arising and ceasing; you also infer that nirvana is eternal bliss, and say there is a body to enjoy it. This is to cling to birth and death and to be attached to worldly pleasures."

You should now know that the Buddha, because all deluded people take the union of the five aggregates as the form of a self, discriminate all dharmas as the forms of external dusts, love life and hate death, drift thought after thought, not knowing that dream and illusion are false, and suffer transmigration in vain, turning the eternal bliss of nirvana into the form of suffering and running after it all day long, the Buddha, pitying this, revealed the true bliss of nirvana. In an instant there is no mark of arising; in an instant there is no mark of ceasing; there is no longer any arising and ceasing to be extinguished, and this is the still extinction present before one. When it is present, there is no measure of its presence, and this is called eternal bliss. This bliss has neither a receiver nor a non-receiver; how can there be the name of one substance with five functions? How much less can one say that nirvana restrains and subdues all dharmas, so that they never arise? This is to slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. Hear my verse:”
The supreme great nirvana, round and bright, eternally still and shining; the ordinary and foolish call it death, and the heretics hold it to be annihilation.
Those who seek the two vehicles regard it as non-action; all this belongs to the reckonings of feeling, and is the root of the sixty-two views.
Falsely establishing empty names, what is the true meaning? Only the man beyond measure penetrates without grasping or rejecting.
One knows the dharmas of the five aggregates, and the self within them, and the many forms of color that appear without, and every sound and mark.
Equal as dream and illusion, one rouses no view of ordinary or sage, makes no interpretation of nirvana; the two extremes and the three times are cut off.
Constantly responding to the functions of the sense faculties, yet without an arising thought of function; discriminating all dharmas, yet without an arising thought of discrimination.
When the fire of the kalpa burns the ocean's depths and the wind drives the mountains to crash, the true eternal still-extinction bliss is nirvana's mark even so.
I now force words to speak, to make you abandon the evil view; do not follow the words in your understanding, and I will grant you a little share of knowing.”
Zhidao heard the verse, was greatly enlightened, leapt up, made a bow, and withdrew.

The Chan Master Xingsi was born of the Liu family in Ancheng of Jizhou. Hearing of the flourishing teaching of the Dharma seat at Caoxi, he came straight to pay his respects, and asked, "What should one apply himself to, that he may fall on no stage?" The Master said, "What have you been doing?" He said, "Not even the holy truth is done." The Master said, "Then on what stage do you fall?" He said, "Since even the holy truth is not done, what stage could there be?" The Master valued him deeply, and asked Xingsi to lead the assembly. One day the Master said to him, "You should spread the teaching in one region, and not let it be cut off." Once Xingsi had gained the Dharma, he returned to Mount Qingyuan in Jizhou, and spread the Dharma, continuing the teaching.

blocks.text: 12. To Say It Is Like a Thing

inline.s: The Chan Master Huairang was a son of the Du family of Jinzhou. At first he went to pay respects to the National Master Hui'an of Mount Song, and Hui'an sent him to Caoxi to inquire. When Huairang arrived he bowed. The Master said, "Whence have you come?" He said, "From Mount Song." The Master said, "What thing is it, thus come?" He said, "If one says it is like a thing, it misses." The Master said, "May it still be cultivated and realized?" He said, "As for cultivation and realization there is none; as for defilement there is no obtaining." The Master said, "This very non-defilement is what all the Buddhas guard and keep in mind. Since you are thus, I am thus too. In the West, Prajnatara prophesied that from beneath your feet shall come a colt that will trample the people of the world to death. It lies in your mind; there is no need to speak of it quickly." Huairang was suddenly in accord, and served at the Master's side for fifteen years, advancing daily into the mysterious. Later he went to the Southern Peak, and greatly spread the Chan school.

The Chan Master Xuanjue of Yongjia was a son of the Dai family of Wenzhou. In youth he studied the scriptures and treatises, and was skillful in the Tiantai methods of calm-abiding and contemplation. Through reading the Vimalakirti Sutra he awakened to the ground of the mind. It happened that a disciple of the Master, Xuanche, came to visit him, and in deep converse his words secretly matched the patriarchs. Xuanche said, "Virtuous one, you have gained the Dharma, who is your teacher?" He said, "In the scriptures and treatises I listened to, each had its own transmission. Later, in the Vimalakirti Sutra, I awakened to the mind-seal of the Buddha, but there is no one to certify it." Xuanche said, "Before Bhadraraja the king of wondrous sound it would do; but after Bhadraraja, to awaken without a teacher is all a natural heresy." He said, "I pray you, kind sir, certify me!" Xuanche said, "My words are light; at Caoxi there is the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Master, to whom the four quarters gather like clouds, and all of them are receivers of the Dharma. If you go, we will go together."

Xuanjue then came with Xuanche to visit, circled the Master three times, and stood shaking his staff. The Master said, "A monk should possess the three thousand deportments and the eighty thousand minor practices. Great and honored one, from where have you come, that you give rise to such lofty pride?" Xuanjue said, "The matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift." The Master said, "Why not realize the unborn, and comprehend that there is no swiftness?" He said, "The realization itself is the unborn; the comprehension is fundamentally without swiftness." The Master said, "Indeed! Indeed!"

Xuanjue then composed himself in all deportments and made his bow. After a moment he took his leave. The Master said, "Returning too swiftly?" He said, "I am originally not moving; how could there be swiftness?" The Master said, "Who knows it is not moving?" He said, "It is the kind one himself who gives rise to discrimination." The Master said, "You have well grasped the meaning of the unborn." He said, "Does the unborn have a meaning?" The Master said, "If there is no meaning, who is it that discriminates?" He said, "Discrimination too is not a meaning." The Master said, "Excellent! Stay for a single night." Thereupon he was called One-Night Awakening. Later he wrote the Song of Realizing the Way, which spread greatly throughout the world.

The Chan practitioner Zhihuang at first visited the Fifth Patriarch, and considered that he had attained right absorption, dwelling in a hut, sitting long, for twenty years. Xuanche, a disciple of the Master, wandering to the northern region and hearing of Zhihuang's fame, went to his hut and asked, "What are you doing here?" Zhihuang said, "Entering samadhi." Xuanche said, "You speak of entering samadhi: do you enter with a mind, or without a mind? If without a mind, then all insentient things, grass, trees, tiles, and stones, should all attain samadhi. If with a mind, then all sentient beings with consciousness should all attain samadhi." Zhihuang said, "When I am actually entering samadhi, I do not see any mind of having or non-having." Xuanche said, "Not seeing the mind of having or non-having is itself constant samadhi; how could there be entering and leaving? If there is entering and leaving, that is not the great samadhi." Zhihuang had no reply. After a long while he asked, "Whose line do you hold?" Xuanche said, "My teacher is the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi." Zhihuang said, "What does the Sixth Patriarch take as Chan-samadhi?" Xuanche said, "What my teacher speaks: the wondrous and profound, round and still, with substance and function thus and thus. The five aggregates are originally empty; the six dusts are not existent; without going out or coming in, without samadhi or confusion. The nature of Chan has no abiding, and is free of the abiding in the stillness of Chan; the nature of Chan is unborn, and is free of the arising of Chan thoughts. The mind is like empty space, yet without the measure of empty space."

Zhihuang heard this and came directly to visit the Master. The Master asked, "Virtuous one, why have you come?" Zhihuang related the former circumstances fully. The Master said, "Just as it was said: you have only to make your mind like empty space, without clinging to a view of emptiness, applying it without obstruction, having no mind in movement or stillness, forgetting the feelings of ordinary beings and sages, doing away with subject and object alike, with nature and form thus and thus, there is no time without samadhi." Zhihuang was then greatly enlightened, and the mind he had attained over twenty years left no trace at all. That night, the scholars and commonfolk of the north heard a sound in the sky saying, "Chan Master Zhihuang has today attained the Way!" Zhihuang later took his leave and returned to the north, there to teach and transform the four assemblies.

blocks.text: 15. I Do Not Understand the Buddha's Dharma

inline.s: A monk asked the Master, "The meaning of Huangmei, who has obtained it?" The Master said, "The one who understands the Buddha's Dharma obtains it." The monk said, "Has the Master obtained it then?" The Master said, "I do not understand the Buddha's Dharma."

One day the Master wished to wash the robe he had received, but there was no good spring, so he went behind the temple about a li or five, and saw the mountains and woods luxuriant, with auspicious vapor coiling about them. The Master struck the ground with his staff, and a spring gushed out at once, gathering into a pool, and he knelt and washed his robe on a stone. Suddenly a monk came to bow, saying, "Fangbian is from Western Shu. Yesterday, in the southern land of India, I saw the Patriarch Bodhidharma, who charged Fangbian to hasten to the land of Tang: "I have transmitted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the samghati robe to Mahakashyapa; it is now handed down to the sixth generation at Caoxi in Shaozhou. Go and pay your respects." Fangbian has come from afar, hoping to see the robe and bowl my master has transmitted." The Master then showed them to him.

Then he asked, "What craft does the venerable one practice?" He said, "I am skilled at sculpting." The Master, with a stern face, said, "Try to sculpture it and let me see." Fangbian was at a loss. After several days he sculpted a true image, about seven inches high, capturing the utmost of its wonder. The Master smiled and said, "You understand only the nature of sculpture, not the Buddha-nature." The Master stretched out his hand and stroked Fangbian's head, saying, "Be forever the field of blessing for gods and men!" And he still gave him the robe as a reward.

Fangbian took the robe and divided it into three: one part he draped on the image, one he kept for himself, and one he wrapped in palm fiber and buried in the earth, vowing, "When this robe is found thereafter, it will be my arising in the world; I will take up the abbotship here and rebuild the halls."

(In the eighth year of the Jiayou era of the Song, a monk named Weixian, when repairing the hall and digging the ground, found the robe as fresh as new. The image is at the Gaoquan Temple, and prayers before it were ever answered.)
A monk cited the verse of the Chan Master Wolun:
Wolun has a skill; he can cut off a hundred thoughts,
before the realm his mind does not rise, and bodhi grows daily.”
The Master, hearing it, said, "This verse has not clarified the ground of the mind; if one follows it, it is to add bonds." So he showed a verse:
Huineng has no skill; he does not cut off a hundred thoughts,
before the realm his mind rises again and again; how then does bodhi grow?”

blocks.text: 1. The Southern Huineng and the Northern Shenxiu

inline.s: At that time the Patriarch dwelt at Baolin on Caoxi, and Master Shenxiu was at Yuquan Temple in Jingnan. In those days the two schools flourished, and all people called them the Southern Huineng and the Northern Shenxiu, and so there came to be the division into the two schools of south and north, sudden and gradual; yet the students did not know the aim of the school.

The Master said to the assembly, "The Dharma is originally one school; there are people of south and north. The Dharma is one kind; there are views that are quick and slow. What is called sudden and gradual? The Dharma is neither sudden nor gradual; it is people who are sharp and dull, and so it is called sudden and gradual."

Yet the followers of Shenxiu often mocked the patriarch of the Southern school, saying, "He does not know a single character, what excellence can he have?" Shenxiu said, "He has obtained the wisdom that is without a teacher, and deeply comprehends the supreme vehicle; I am not his equal. Moreover, my teacher the Fifth Patriarch personally transmitted the robe and Dharma to him, surely it was not in vain! I grieve that I cannot go far to draw near to him, but have received the imperial favor in vain. You people should not linger here; you may go to Caoxi to consult and settle it."
One day he told his disciple Zhicheng, "You are clever and wise; you can go to Caoxi for me to hear the Dharma. If you hear anything, record it with all your heart, and come back and tell me."

Zhicheng, obeying the command, went to Caoxi and joined the assembly in their inquiries, without telling whence he came. At that time the Patriarch said to the assembly, "There is a thief of the Dharma now hiding in this gathering." Zhicheng came forth and bowed, and related the whole matter. The Master said, "You come from Yuquan; you must be a spy." He replied, "I am not!" The Master said, "How can you say you are not?" He replied, "Before I spoke, yes; having spoken, no."

The Master said, "What does your teacher show the assembly?" He replied, "He constantly instructs the assembly to abide the mind and contemplate stillness, sitting long without lying down." The Master said, "To abide the mind and contemplate stillness is an illness, not Chan; to sit long and constrain the body, what benefit is that to the principle? Hear my verse:"
Living, one sits and does not lie down; dying, one lies down and does not sit;
a single stinking mass of bones, what set practice do you establish?”

blocks.text: 2. The Dharma of Precepts, Samadhi, and Wisdom

inline.s: Zhicheng bowed again and said, "Your disciple studied the Way under Master Shenxiu for nine years without attaining accord and awakening. Now, upon hearing the Master speak, I am in accord with my original mind. The matter of birth and death is great; I beg the Master, in his great compassion, to instruct me further." The Master said, "I have heard that your teacher instructs students in the Dharma of precepts, samadhi, and wisdom. I do not know how your teacher speaks of precepts, samadhi, and wisdom; tell me." Zhicheng said, "Master Shenxiu says: ‘Not to commit all evils is called precepts; to practice all good is called wisdom; to purify one’s own mind is called samadhi.’ That is how he speaks; I do not know how the Master teaches people."

The Master said, "If I said there is a Dharma to give to people, I would be deceiving you. I only untie the knots according to the occasion, giving the provisional name of samadhi. What your teacher speaks of as precepts, samadhi, and wisdom is truly beyond thought; but what I see as precepts, samadhi, and wisdom is different." Zhicheng said, "Precepts, samadhi, and wisdom should be but one kind; how are they separate?" The Master said, "Your teacher’s precepts, samadhi, and wisdom gather those of the great vehicle; my precepts, samadhi, and wisdom gather those of the supreme vehicle. Since the awakening and understanding differ, the views are quick and slow. Listen to my words, and see if they are the same as his. The Dharma I speak does not depart from the self-nature; to speak the Dharma apart from the substance is called speaking of marks, in which the self-nature is ever deluded. You should know that all the myriad dharmas function from the self-nature, and this is the true Dharma of precepts, samadhi, and wisdom. Hear my verse:"
In the mind-ground no wrong is the precept of the self-nature; in the mind-ground no folly is the wisdom of the self-nature;
in the mind-ground no confusion is the samadhi of the self-nature; neither increasing nor decreasing is the diamond self,
going and coming, body and body, in the very samadhi.”
Zhicheng heard the verse, repented, and thanked him, then offered a verse:
The illusory body of the five aggregates, how could illusion reach the ultimate?
Returning toward true Suchness, the Dharma is still not pure.”

The Master approved. Again he said to Zhicheng, "Your teacher’s precepts, samadhi, and wisdom are for small faculties and small wisdom; my precepts, samadhi, and wisdom are for great faculties and great wisdom. If one awakens to the self-nature, he then neither establishes bodhi nor nirvana, and does not establish liberation or knowledge-and-vision; with no single dharma obtainable, he is then able to establish the myriad dharmas. If you understand this meaning, it is also called the Buddha-body, also called bodhi and nirvana, also called liberation, knowledge, and vision. One who sees nature may establish and it is well, and may not establish and it is well; coming and going freely, without stagnation or obstruction. Applying as occasion requires, responding to words as occasion answers, universally manifesting transformation bodies without departing from the self-nature, he attains the free and unimpeded spiritual powers, sporting in samadhi, and this is called seeing nature."

Zhicheng again asked the Master, "What is the meaning of not establishing?" The Master said, "The self-nature has no wrong, no folly, no confusion; thought after thought prajna contemplates and illuminates, ever free of the marks of dharmas, free and at ease, attaining all at will in every direction, what is there to establish? The self-nature awakens itself; sudden awakening and sudden practice, with no gradualism; therefore no dharma whatsoever is established. All dharmas are still and extinct, what sequence is there?" Zhicheng bowed, and wished to serve at the Master’s side, morning and evening, without slackening.

The monk Zhiche was a native of Jiangxi, his family name Zhang, his name Xingchang. In youth he was a knight-errant. Ever since the division into south and north, though the two patriarchs had no thought of self and other, their followers competed in love and hate. At that time the followers of the northern school set up Master Shenxiu as the Sixth Patriarch on their own, and, resenting that the Patriarch’s transmission of the robe was famed throughout the world, they charged Xingchang to come and assassinate the Master.

The Master’s mind was penetrating, and he foreknew the matter, so he set ten taels of gold beside his seat. At nightfall Xingchang entered the Patriarch’s room and was about to harm him. The Master stretched out his neck to meet the blade; Xingchang swung the knife three times, but nothing was harmed at all. The Master said, "The right sword is not untrue; the untrue sword is not right; I owe you only gold, and not your life!" Xingchang, startled, fell prostrate, and only after a long while came to himself, then begged pity, repented his fault, and wished to leave the household life. The Master thereupon gave him the gold, saying, "Go away for now; I fear the assembly may turn and harm you. On another day you may come with a changed appearance, and I will receive you." Xingchang, obeying, fled by night, and later took refuge as a monk, receiving the full precepts and practicing diligently.

blocks.text: 5. The Meaning of Eternal and Impermanent

inline.s: One day, recalling the Master’s words, he came from afar to pay his respects. The Master said, "I have long thought of you; why have you come so late?" He said, "Yesterday I received the Master’s pardon of my offense. Though I have now left the household life and practice austerities, it is still hard to repay your kindness; the only way is to transmit the Dharma and save beings! Your disciple has often read the Nirvana Sutra, but does not understand the meaning of eternal and impermanent; I beg the Master, in compassion, to explain it briefly."

The Master said, "What is impermanent is precisely the Buddha-nature; what is eternal is precisely all the good and evil dharmas and the discriminating mind." He said, "What the Master says is greatly against the text of the sutra." The Master said, "I transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal; how could I dare to go against the Buddha’s scripture?" He said, "The sutra says the Buddha-nature is eternal, yet the Master says it is impermanent; good and evil dharmas, even the bodhi-mind, are all impermanent, yet the Master says they are constant. This is contrary, and makes the student all the more doubtful." The Master said, "When I formerly heard the nun Wujincang recite the Nirvana Sutra once, I then expounded it, and there was not a single word or principle contrary to the text; even for you, there will be no second explanation." He said, "Your student’s knowledge is shallow and unclear; I beg the Master to explain it fully and compassionately."

The Master said, "Do you know? If the Buddha-nature were eternal, what would there be to say about good and evil dharmas? Even to the end of a kalpa, there would be no one who roused the bodhi-mind. Therefore when I say it is impermanent, this is precisely the Buddha’s teaching of the true eternal Way. Again, if all dharmas were impermanent, then each thing would have its own self-nature capable of receiving birth and death, and the true eternal nature would have places where it is not pervasive. Therefore when I say it is constant, this is precisely the Buddha’s meaning of true impermanence. The Buddha, because ordinary beings and heretics cling to a false eternalism, and those of the two vehicles reckon the eternal as impermanent, together making eight upside-down views, therefore in the ultimate-meaning teaching of nirvana he breaks those one-sided views and reveals the true eternal, true bliss, true self, and true purity. Now, clinging to the words while opposing the meaning, taking annihilation-impermanence and a fixed dead-eternalism, you misread the Buddha’s subtle final words, even if you scan them a thousand times, what benefit is there?"
Xingchang suddenly was greatly enlightened, and spoke a verse:
Because one holds to the impermanent mind, the Buddha speaks of the eternal nature;
one who does not understand the expedient means is like gathering pebbles from a spring pool.
Now without expending effort, the Buddha-nature appears before me;
if it were not that the Master bestowed it, I could have had nothing attained.”
The Master said, "You are now thoroughly penetrated; you should be named Zhiche." Zhiche bowed in thanks and withdrew.

blocks.text: 6. Shenhui Comes to Pay His Respects

inline.s: There was a young lad named Shenhui, a son of the Gao family of Xiangyang, thirteen years old, who came from Yuquan to pay his respects. The Master said, "This good friend has come a long way in hardship; have you still brought your original nature? If you have the original, you should recognize the master; try and speak." Shenhui said, "Taking non-abiding as the original, seeing is the master." The Master said, "This young novice, how can he speak such offhand words?" Shenhui then asked, "Master, when you sit in meditation, do you see or not?" The Master struck him three times with his staff and said, "When I strike you, does it hurt or not?" He replied, "It both hurts and does not hurt." The Master said, "I both see and do not see." Shenhui asked, "How is this ‘both seeing and not seeing’?"

The Master said, "What I see: I constantly see the faults of my own mind, and do not see the right and wrong, the likes and dislikes, of others; therefore I both see and do not see. You say ‘it both hurts and does not hurt’, how so? If you do not hurt, you are the same as wood and stone; if it hurts, you are the same as an ordinary person, and then you give rise to anger and hate. What you earlier asked, seeing and not seeing, is a pair of extremes; pain and non-pain is arising and ceasing. You have not even seen your own self-nature, and yet dare to toy with people?" Shenhui bowed and repented, thanking him.

The Master further said, "If your mind is deluded and cannot see, ask a good friend of the Dharma to find the path; if your mind is awakened, you see your own nature and practice according to the Dharma. You are deluded and cannot see your own mind, yet you come to ask me about seeing and not seeing. My seeing is known by me; how can it stand in for your delusion? If you see for yourself, neither can it stand in for my delusion. Why not know and see for yourself, and instead ask me about seeing and not seeing?" Shenhui bowed again over a hundred times, seeking pardon for his fault, and served diligently, never leaving the Master’s side.

One day the Master said to the assembly, "I have a thing: no head, no tail; no name, no word; no back, no face. Do you recognize it?" Shenhui came forth and said, "It is the source of all Buddhas, the Buddha-nature of Shenhui." The Master said, "I told you it has no name and no word, and you at once call it the source and the Buddha-nature. Hereafter, though you may have a thatch to cover your head, you will only become a follower of understanding and interpretation."

After the Patriarch’s passing, Shenhui entered the capital Luoyang, and greatly spread the sudden teaching of Caoxi, writing the Record on Manifesting the School, which circulated widely in the world.

The Master saw that the followers of the various schools, given to difficult questioning, had all stirred up malicious minds and gathered in great numbers beneath his seat. Moved to compassion, he said to them: “Those who study the Way should altogether wipe out all good thought and evil thought. Being nameless, name it after the self-nature; the non-dual nature is called the true nature. Upon that true nature all the teaching-gates are established, and at the very words you must see it for yourselves.” Hearing this, the assembled people all paid their respects, requesting to serve the Master as their teacher.

blocks.text: Chapter Nine: The Chapter on Protecting the Dharma
1. The Speedy Edict Summoning the Master

inline.s: On the festival of the first full moon of the first year of the Shenlong era, Empress Wu Zetian and Emperor Zhongzong issued an edict saying: “We have invited the two masters An and Xiu to be supported in the palace. In the leisure of the myriad affairs of state, We constantly investigate the One Vehicle. The two masters deferring, said: ‘In the south there is a Chan master Neng, who received in secret the robe and the Dharma of the great master Ren and transmits the Buddha’s mind-seal; he may be invited and questioned.’ Now We send the inner attendant Xue Jian with a speeding edict to invite you. We beg the Master, in his compassion, to come quickly to the capital.” The Master presented a memorial declining on the ground of illness, wishing to end his days amid the forests and hills.

blocks.text: 2. Sitting in Meditation and Entering Concentration

inline.s: Xue Jian said: “The Chan worthies of the capital all say: ‘To attain the Way one must sit in meditation and enter concentration; one who is liberated without relying on meditation and concentration has never existed.’ We have not yet heard what Dharma the Master teaches.” The Master said: “The Way is awakened to by the mind — how could it be in sitting? The Sutra says: If one says the Tathagata sits or lies down, he is practicing an erroneous path. Why? Since he has no coming from anywhere and no going to anywhere. No arising and no ceasing — this is the Tathagata’s pure meditation. All dharmas are empty and still — this is the Tathagata’s pure sitting. In the ultimate there is nothing to realize; how much less so a mere sitting!”

blocks.text: 3. Pointing Out the Essence of the Mind

inline.s: Xue Jian said: “When the disciple returns to the capital, the sovereign will certainly question me. I beg the Master, in his compassion, to point out the essence of the mind, so that I may transmit and report it to the two palaces and to those in the capital who study the Way. It is like one lamp lighting a hundred thousand lamps: the dark ones are all illuminated, and the illumination is endless.” The Master said: “The Way has neither brightness nor darkness; brightness and darkness are the meaning of mutual alternation. That the illumination is endless is also to call it finite, because the name is established in mutual dependence. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: The Dharma has no comparison, because it has nothing to depend upon.”

Xue Jian said: “Brightness is the metaphor for wisdom, and darkness for affliction. If a person who cultivates the Way does not use wisdom to break through affliction, then on what can he rely to escape the beginningless birth and death?” The Master said: “Affliction is itself bodhi; they are not two and not separate. To use wisdom to break affliction — this is the view of the two vehicles, the capacity of the goat and the deer. Superior wisdom and great faculties are altogether not like this.” Xue Jian said: “What is the view of the Mahayana?” The Master said: “Brightness and non-brightness: the ordinary person sees them as two; the wise know thoroughly that their nature is not dual. The non-dual nature is the true nature. The true nature is not diminished amid the common and foolish, not increased in the sage and worthy; abiding amid affliction it is not disturbed, dwelling in concentration it is not stilled. It is neither interrupted nor eternal, neither coming nor going, neither within the middle nor without and within, neither arising nor ceasing. Nature and marks are as such, abiding and unchanging — this is called the Way.”

Xue Jian said: “The Master speaks of no arising and no ceasing — how is this different from the heresy of the externalists?” The Master said: “What the externalists call no arising and no ceasing is to use ceasing to stop arising and to use arising to reveal ceasing: their ceasing is still not ceasing, and their arising they call not arising. What I call no arising and no ceasing is: originally there was no arising, and now there is no ceasing, and therefore it is different from the externalists. If you wish to know the essence of the mind, do but refrain from thinking of any good or evil, and you will naturally enter the pure essence of mind, serene and eternally still, with its wonderful functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.” Xue Jian, having received the instruction, was suddenly and completely enlightened; he bowed, took leave, and returned to the palace, presenting the Master’s words in his memorial.

On the third day of the ninth month of that year, an edict commended the Master, saying: “The Master has declined on account of old age and illness, and, cultivating the Way for Us, is a field of blessing for the nation. The Master, like Vimalakirti, feigning illness at Vaishali, has proclaimed the Mahayana, transmitted the mind of all Buddhas, and spoken the Dharma of non-duality. Xue Jian transmitted the Master’s instruction on the Tathagata’s knowledge and vision. We have gathered the surplus blessings of accumulated virtue and planted the roots of goodness in past lives; encountering the Master’s appearance in the world, We suddenly awaken to the Supreme Vehicle. Mindful of the Master’s grace, We bow our heads in endless gratitude! And We offer the woolen kasaya and the crystal bowl, and command the prefect of Shaozhou to restore the monastery buildings and present the Master’s former dwelling as the Guoen (Nation’s Grace) monastery.”

blocks.text: Chapter Ten: The Chapter of Entrustment
1. Teaching You to Speak the Dharma

inline.s: One day the Master called his disciples Fahai, Zhicheng, Fada, Shenhui, Zhichang, Zhitong, Zhizhe, Zhidao, Fazhen, and Faru, and said: “You are not like the rest of people; after my nirvana, each of you will be a master of one direction. I now teach you to speak the Dharma so as not to lose the fundamental school. First you must raise the three categories of dharmas, employ the thirty-six pairs of opposites, and in going out and coming in remain far from the two extremes; in expounding all dharmas do not depart from the self-nature. If someone suddenly asks you about the Dharma, let your words be in pairs, always taking up the dharma of the opposites, with coming and going mutually dependent; in the end the two dharmas are entirely done away with, and there is nowhere further to go.”

The three categories of dharmas are the aggregates, the realms, and the entrances. The aggregates are the five aggregates, namely form, feeling, thought, mental formations, and consciousness. The entrances are the twelve entrances: the six external sense-dusts — form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharma; and the six internal gates — eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The realms are the eighteen realms: the six sense-dusts, the six gates, and the six consciousnesses.

The self-nature can contain the myriad dharmas; this is called the alaya (store-house) consciousness. If thinking arises, this is the evolving consciousness. From it arise the six consciousnesses, which go out through the six gates and see the six sense-dusts; thus the eighteen realms all function from the self-nature. If the self-nature is evil, there arise eighteen evils; if the self-nature is right, there arise eighteen rightnesses. If one uses it in evil, it is the use of sentient beings; if one uses it in good, it is the use of the Buddha. Of what does the use consist? Of the self-nature itself.

The dharma of the opposites. Five pairs of the insentient external realms: with heaven, with earth; with sun, with moon; with brightness, with darkness; with yin, with yang; with water, with fire — these are the five pairs.

Twelve pairs of dharma-marks and language: with words, with dharma; with being, with nonbeing; with possessing form, with formlessness; with possessing marks, with marklessness; with the defiled, with the undefiled; with form, with emptiness; with motion, with stillness; with purity, with turbidity; with the ordinary, with the holy; with monks, with laypeople; with old, with young; with great, with small — these are the twelve pairs.

Nineteen pairs in the functions of the self-nature: with long, with short; with evil, with right; with delusion, with wisdom; with foolish, with wise; with confusion, with concentration; with compassion, with malice; with precepts, with non-precepts; with straight, with crooked; with real, with false; with dangerous, with level; with affliction, with bodhi; with constant, with inconstant; with pity, with harm; with joy, with anger; with renunciation, with stinginess; with advance, with retreat; with arising, with ceasing; with the Dharma-body, with the physical body; with the transformation-body, with the reward-body — these are the nineteen pairs.”

The Master said: “If you understand how to employ these thirty-six pairs of opposites, then the Way will be threaded through all the scriptures and dharmas, and in going out and coming in you will be far from the two extremes. When the self-nature functions and you converse with others, be apart from marks amid outer marks, and be apart from emptiness amid inner emptiness. If you cling entirely to marks, you will grow erroneous views; if you hold entirely to emptiness, you will grow ignorance. A person who holds to emptiness slanders the scriptures, flatly saying there is no need of words. Since he says there is no need of words, then people should not speak at all — for this very speech is the mark of words. Again he says: ‘The direct way establishes no words.’ But these very two characters ‘no words’ are themselves words. When he sees what others say, he immediately slanders them as clinging to words. You should know that to be deluded oneself is one thing, but to slander the Buddha’s scriptures is another. Do not slander the scriptures, for the offense and hindrance are immeasurable!”

If one clings to marks outside and does work to seek the true, or widely builds up teaching grounds and speaks of the faults of being and nonbeing, such a person will not see the nature even over many kalpas. Just listen and practice in accord with the Dharma, and do not cease to think of the hundred things and thereby obstruct the way-nature. If you listen and do not practice, you will cause people to give rise to false thoughts. Just practice in accord with the Dharma and give the Dharma-gift without dwelling on marks. If you awaken, and speak thus, use thus, practice thus, and act thus, you will not lose the fundamental school.

If someone asks you about the meaning: when asked about being, answer with nonbeing; when asked about nonbeing, answer with being; when asked about the ordinary, answer with the holy; when asked about the holy, answer with the ordinary. The two paths are mutually dependent, and the meaning of the Middle Way is produced. As with one question answered with one pair, all remaining questions are handled in this manner, and you will not lose the principle. Suppose someone asks: ‘What is meant by darkness?’ Answer: Brightness is the cause and darkness the condition; when brightness ceases there is darkness. Use brightness to reveal darkness and darkness to reveal brightness; coming and going are mutually dependent, forming the meaning of the Middle Way. All remaining questions are all like this. You who are to transmit the Dharma hereafter should teach by turning this over and over, and not lose the essential purport!”

In the first year of the Taiji era (renzi), in the seventh month of the Yanhe period, the Master commanded his disciples to go to the Guoen Monastery in Xinzhou to build a stupa, and urged that the work be hastened. In the following year, at the end of summer, it was completed. On the first day of the seventh month he gathered the assembly and said: “In the eighth month I wish to leave the world. If you have doubts, ask me early, and I will resolve them for you and let your confusion be entirely ended. After I am gone, no one will teach you!” Hearing this, Fahai and the others all wept; only Shenhui was unmoved in his spirit, and did not weep.

The Master said: “The young master Shenhui alone has attained the equality of good and evil, is unmoved by slander and praise, and gives rise to neither grief nor joy. The rest of you have not attained this. After years in the mountains, what Way have you cultivated? Why do you grieve and weep now — for whom is the anxiety? If you grieve that I do not know where I am going, I know where I am going; if I did not know where I am going, I would not have told you in advance. Your weeping is because you do not know where I go; if you knew where I go, you would not weep. For the Dharma-nature is originally without arising or ceasing, without coming or going.”

blocks.text: 5. The Verse on True and False, Motion and Stillness

inline.s: Sit down, all of you, and I will speak to you a verse called the ‘Verse on True and False, Motion and Stillness.’ When you have learned and recited this verse, you will be of one mind with me; practicing in accord with it, you will not lose the essential purport!”
The assembled monks paid their respects and asked the Master to compose the verse. The verse says:
In all things there is nothing true; do not take it for the seeing of the true;
If one sees it as the true, what he sees is altogether not true.
If one can possess the true of himself, apart from the false the mind is true;
If the self-mind does not leave the false, where is the true to be found in what has no truth?
Sentient beings are those who comprehend motion; the insentient are those without motion;
If one practices the practice of immobility, he is the same as the insentient, without motion.
If you seek the true immobility, in motion there is immobility;
If immobility is just immobility, then the insentient have no seed of Buddhahood.
Able to distinguish the marks well, in the truth of the First Meaning there is no motion;
But if you have such a view, that is the function of Suchness.
I tell all who study the Way: make effort and be attentive;
Do not, at the gate of the Mahayana, cling to the wisdom of birth and death.
If at the words there is correspondence, then together discuss the meaning of the Buddha;
If in truth there is no correspondence, put palms together and let the other be glad.
This school is originally without contention; contention is to lose the meaning of the Way;
To cling to the perverse Dharma-door of contention, one’s self-nature enters birth and death.”

At that time, having heard the verse, the assembly of followers all paid their respects and, comprehending the Master’s meaning, each gathered his mind and practiced in accord with the Dharma, daring no longer to contend.

blocks.text: 6. The Platform Sutra of the Dharma Treasure

inline.s: Then they knew the Master would not long remain in the world. The Elder Fahai bowed again and asked: “After the Master’s nirvana, to whom shall the robe and the Dharma be entrusted?” The Master said: “When I spoke the Dharma at the Dafan Monastery up to the present, the record has been copied and circulated, and is called the Platform Sutra of the Dharma Treasure. You should guard it and transmit it to one another, delivering all beings; as long as you expound in accord with this, it is called the true Dharma. Now I speak the Dharma for you, but I no longer bequeath the robe, because the root of your faith is pure and ripe, your determination beyond doubt, worthy to shoulder the great matter. Yet according to the verse of entrustment of the ancestor Bodhidharma, the robe should not be transmitted. The verse says:”
I originally came to this land, transmitting the Dharma to save the deluded;
One flower opens into five leaves; the fruit is naturally accomplished.”

blocks.text: 7. The Single Mark and the Single Practice

inline.s: The Master further said: “Good friends! Each of you should purify your mind and listen to my speaking the Dharma. If you wish to accomplish the wisdom of all species, you must reach the samadhi of the single mark and the samadhi of the single practice. If in all places you do not dwell in marks, and in those marks give rise to neither hatred nor love, have neither grasping nor rejection, and do not think of benefit, success, or failure and the like, being at ease, tranquil, void, calm, and indifferent — this is called the samadhi of the single mark. If in all places, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, you maintain a single straightforward mind, with an unmoved place of the Way and truly accomplish the Pure Land — this is called the samadhi of the single practice. If a person is endowed with these two samadhis, it is like the earth having the seed, which conceals, nourishes, and matures its fruit. The single mark and the single practice are likewise.”

The Dharma I now speak is like the timely rain that universally moistens the great earth; and your Buddha-nature is likened to the seeds, which, meeting this saturation, all sprout. One who receives my purport will certainly attain bodhi; one who practices according to my words will surely realize the wonderful fruit. Listen to my verse:”
The mind-ground contains all the seeds; by the universal rain all sprout;
When the flower of sudden awakening has already so come, the fruit of bodhi is naturally accomplished.”

Having spoken the verse, the Master said: “The Dharma is non-dual, and the mind is likewise so. The Way is pure and also without all marks. Take care not to contemplate stillness, nor to empty the mind; this mind is originally pure, and there is nothing to grasp or reject. Each of you make effort on your own, and, according to conditions, fare well!” At that time the assembled followers paid their respects and withdrew.

blocks.text: 8. The Falling Leaf Returns to the Root

inline.s: On the eighth day of the seventh month, the Master suddenly said to his disciples: “I wish to return to Xinzhou; you should quickly prepare the boat.” The assembly entreated him to remain with great earnestness. The Master said: “Even the Buddhas, appearing in the world, still show nirvana; where there is coming there must be going, and this is the constant principle. This body of mine must have a place to return.” The assembly said: “Master, going from here, will you return soon?” The Master said: “The falling leaf returns to the root; and when I come again, I have no words.” They asked again: “To whom is the true eye-treasury of the Dharma entrusted?” The Master said: “The one who has the Way obtains it; the one who is without mind is versed in it.”

They asked again: “In the future, will there be any peril?” The Master said: “Five or six years after my nirvana, a person will come to take my head. Hear my prophecy: On the head one nurses the parents; in the mouth one needs food. The peril of ‘Man’; the officials of ‘Poplar and Willow.’” Again he said: “Seventy years after I am gone, two bodhisattvas will come from the East, one a renunciant and one a householder; at the same time they will spread the teaching, establish my school, build monasteries, and make the Dharma-succession flourish.”

blocks.text: 9. The Lineage of the Chan School

inline.s: They asked: “We do not know how many generations have been transmitted, from the historically manifested Buddhas and patriarchs down to the present. We beg the Master to disclose it.” The Master said: “The ancient Buddhas who appeared in the world were already without number and cannot be counted. Now we take the seven Buddhas as the beginning. In the past kalpa of Splendor: Vipashyin Buddha, Shikhin Buddha, and Vishvabhu Buddha; in the present kalpa of the Wise: Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kashyapa Buddha, and Shakyamuni Buddha — these are the seven Buddhas.”

Shakyamuni Buddha first transmitted to the Venerable Mahakashyapa; second, the Venerable Ananda; third, the Venerable Shanavasa; fourth, the Venerable Upagupta; fifth, the Venerable Dhritaka; sixth, the Venerable Micchaka; seventh, the Venerable Vasumitra; eighth, the Venerable Buddhanandi; ninth, the Venerable Buddhamitra; tenth, the Venerable Parsva; eleventh, the Venerable Punyayashas; twelfth, the Great Being Ashvaghosha; thirteenth, the Venerable Kapimala; fourteenth, the Great Being Nagarjuna; fifteenth, the Venerable Kanadeva; sixteenth, the Venerable Rahulata; seventeenth, the Venerable Sanghanandi; eighteenth, the Venerable Gayashata; nineteenth, the Venerable Kumarata; twentieth, the Venerable Jayata; twenty-first, the Venerable Vasubandhu; twenty-second, the Venerable Manorhita; twenty-third, the Venerable Haklenayashas; twenty-fourth, the Venerable Simha; twenty-fifth, the Venerable Basiasita; twenty-sixth, the Venerable Punyamitra; twenty-seventh, the Venerable Prajnatara; twenty-eighth, the Venerable Bodhidharma; twenty-ninth, the great master Huike; thirtieth, the great master Sengcan; thirty-first, the great master Daoxin; thirty-second, the great master Hongren; and Huineng is the thirty-third patriarch. The patriarchs of old each had their transmission. You, in the generations to come, should pass it down from teacher to teacher and not err!”

In the Xiantian era, second year (guichou), on the third day of the eighth month, after the meal at the Guoen Monastery, the Master said to his disciples: “Take your places in order, and I will take leave of you.”
Fahai said: “Master, what teaching will you leave, so that the deluded people of later generations may see their Buddha-nature?”

The Master said: “Listen carefully! If the deluded people of later ages recognize sentient beings, that is their Buddha-nature; if they do not recognize sentient beings, then in ten thousand kalpas seeking the Buddha they will hardly encounter him. I now teach you: recognize the sentient beings of your own mind and see the Buddha-nature of your own mind. If you seek to see the Buddha, just recognize sentient beings; for it is only that sentient beings are deluded about the Buddha, not that the Buddha is deluded about sentient beings. If the self-nature awakens, sentient beings are the Buddha; if the self-nature is deluded, the Buddha is sentient beings. If the self-nature is equal, sentient beings are the Buddha; if the self-nature is evil and dangerous, the Buddha is sentient beings. If your mind is dangerous and crooked, then the Buddha is amid sentient beings; with a single thought of straight and even, sentient beings are the Buddha. My own mind has the Buddha in itself; this self-Buddha is the true Buddha. If the self lacks the Buddha-mind, where will you seek a real Buddha? Your self-mind is the Buddha; do not doubt it further. Outside there is no single thing that can be established; all the ten thousand dharmas are born from the original mind. Therefore the Sutra says: When the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of dharmas cease.”

blocks.text: 11. The Verse on the True Buddha of Self-Nature

inline.s: I now leave a verse to take leave of you, called the ‘Verse on the True Buddha of Self-Nature.’ People of later generations, knowing the meaning of this verse, will see their own original mind and accomplish their own path of Buddhahood. The verse says:
Suchness, the self-nature, is the true Buddha; erroneous views and the three poisons are the devil king;
When deluded by error, the devil is in the house; when right views are present, the Buddha is in the hall.
When erroneous views and the three poisons arise in the nature, that is the devil king coming to dwell in the house;
With right views the mind of the three poisons is naturally removed; the devil becomes the Buddha, truly without falsehood.
The Dharma-body, the reward-body, and the transformation-body — these three bodies are originally one body;
If you can see it for yourself within the nature, that is the cause of becoming a Buddha, of bodhi.
Originally from the transformation-body the pure nature is born; the pure nature is always within the transformation-body;
If the nature makes the transformation-body walk the right path, in the future it will be perfected and truly endless.
The nature of lust is originally the cause of the pure nature; apart from lust is the body of the pure nature;
In the nature, when one is freed from the five desires, to see the nature in an instant is to be the true.
In this life, if one meets the gate of the sudden teaching and suddenly awakens to the self-nature, he sees the World-Honored One;
If you seek to practice and find how to become a Buddha, do you know where to seek the true?
If you can see the true within the mind, having the true is the cause of becoming a Buddha;
If you do not see the self-nature and seek the Buddha outside, then whoever raises the mind is always the great fool.
The gate of the sudden teaching is now left behind; to save and deliver the world’s people one must cultivate oneself;
I tell you who are to study the Way in the future: not to have this view is a great remissness.”

blocks.text: 12. Causing You to See Your Nature

inline.s: Having spoken the verse, the Master announced: “Dwell well, all of you! After my nirvana, do not indulge in the world’s grief and shed streaming tears. To receive condolement and put on mourning clothes — such a one is not my disciple, nor is it the true Dharma. Just know your original mind and see your original nature, which is without motion or stillness, without arising or ceasing, without coming or going, without right or wrong, without abiding or departing. I fear that your minds are deluded and will not comprehend my meaning, so I instruct you again, to cause you to see your nature. After my nirvana, practice according to this, exactly as when I was in the world; if you go against my teaching, then even if I were in the world, there would be no benefit.”
Again he spoke a verse, saying:
Unmoved, one does not cultivate good; unrestrained, one does not commit evil;
Still and silent, cutting off seeing and hearing; vast and free, the mind has no attachment.

blocks.text: 13. The White Rainbow Reaching the Ground

inline.s: Having spoken the verse, the Master sat upright until the third watch of the night. Suddenly he said to his disciples: “I go now!” and, calmly, he passed away. At that time rare incense filled the chamber, a white rainbow reached the ground, the trees and woods turned white, and the birds and beasts cried out in grief.

In the eleventh month, the officials of the three prefectures — Guangzhou, Shaozhou, and Xinzhou — together with the disciples, monks, and laypeople, contended to receive the true body, unable to decide where it should go; so they burned incense and prayed: “Wherever the incense-smoke points, there shall the Master abide.” At that time the smoke of the incense went straight through toward Caoxi. On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, they moved the spirit-shrine together with the transmitted robe and bowl and returned.

In the following year, on the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month, they opened the shrine, and the disciple Fangbian applied fragrant clay to the body. The disciples, recalling the prophecy about the taking of the head, first protected the Master’s neck with iron leaves and lacquered cloth, and entered it into the stupa. Suddenly within the stupa a white light appeared, rising straight up into the sky, and only dispersed after three days. The prefecture of Shaozhou reported it to the throne, and an imperial edict was issued to erect a stele recording the Master’s virtuous conduct.

The Master lived to seventy-six. At twenty-four he received the robe; at thirty-nine he shaved his head; and he spoke the Dharma to benefit beings for thirty-seven years. Those who obtained his purport and succeeded to the Dharma numbered forty-three; those who awakened to the Way and transcended the ordinary were beyond counting. The faithful robe transmitted by Bodhidharma, the woolen and jeweled bowl bestowed by Emperor Zhongzong, the true portrait sculpted by Fangbian, and the implements — these the keeper of the stupa preserved, to be forever safeguarded at the Baolin way-place. The Platform Sutra was circulated in order to reveal the essential purport. All these are matters that caused the Triple Gem to flourish and universally benefited all beings.
